blocks.text:
Up to now we treated Redis as a black box that answers commands quickly. This Part opens the box. Understanding what the server does between "bytes arrive on a socket" and "reply leaves the socket" lets you predict behaviour instead of memorising it: why one slow command stalls every client, why `UNLINK` exists next to `DEL`, why a `BGSAVE` can make latency spike, and why more CPU cores do not make a single Redis instance run commands in parallel.

This chapter covers the process anatomy (threads and child processes), the event loop, the life of one command, the I/O threads, and the practical consequences for latency. The chapters that follow zoom into memory, expiry, eviction and persistence.

### One process, a few threads, occasional children

A running `redis-server` is one operating-system process. Inside it you will find:

- **The main thread.** It runs the event loop, parses client requests, executes every command against the dataset, and (in the classic design) writes replies. All reads and writes of your keys happen here, one command at a time. This is why Redis needs no locks around its data structures.
- **I/O threads (optional).** Helper threads that move bytes between sockets and buffers. They never touch the dataset. Disabled by default.
- **Background threads (always there).** Small worker threads for jobs that would block the main thread: closing files, calling `fsync` on the AOF, and freeing big objects (lazy free). Redis calls this subsystem *bio* (background I/O).
- **Child processes (occasionally).** When Redis writes an RDB snapshot or rewrites the AOF, it calls `fork()`. The child process writes the file while the parent keeps serving clients.

**Threads and processes of one Redis server**

blocks.code:
┌────────────────────────── redis-server (parent process) ─────────────────────────┐
│                                                                                   │
│  main thread        : event loop, parse, EXECUTE COMMANDS, timers (serverCron)   │
│  I/O threads (opt.) : read/parse and write sockets, no dataset access            │
│  bio threads        : close(fd), fsync(AOF), lazy free of big objects            │
│                                                                                   │
└───────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │ fork()  (only during BGSAVE / BGREWRITEAOF / some replica syncs)
                ▼
        ┌──────────────────┐
        │  child process   │  writes dump.rdb or the new AOF base file, then exits
        └──────────────────┘

blocks.text:
The key sentence to remember: **commands run on one thread**. Everything else in the picture exists to keep that one thread from waiting.

### The event loop

Redis is *event driven*. Instead of one thread per client, which would need locks and many stacks, a single loop asks the operating system "which of my sockets are ready?" and handles only those. The library that implements this is called **ae** (a simple event library written for Redis). On Linux it uses `epoll`; on BSD and macOS it uses `kqueue`; other systems fall back to `evport` or `select`. The technique is called I/O multiplexing.

The loop handles two kinds of events:

- **File events**: a socket became readable (a client sent bytes, or a new client is connecting) or writable (room to send a reply).
- **Time events**: periodic jobs, chiefly `serverCron`, which runs `hz` times per second (default `hz 10`, so every 100 ms). It does housekeeping: the active expire cycle, incremental rehashing of big dictionaries, client timeouts, checking if a background save finished, and updating statistics.

**One turn of the event loop (simplified pseudocode)**

Note that "execute" sits inside the loop body. While a command runs, the loop does not turn: no other client is read, no reply is sent, no timer fires. A command that takes 10 ms therefore adds up to 10 ms of waiting to every other client that arrived during it.

### The life of one command

Take the command `HSET product:1001 name "Mug" price 1299` sent by a ShopStream catalog-service. These are the steps on the server.

1. **Accept and register.** When the connection was opened, Redis created a *client* structure for it: a query buffer (bytes received but not yet consumed), an output buffer (replies waiting to be sent), the selected database, the authenticated user, and so on.
2. **Read.** The socket becomes readable. Redis reads available bytes into the client's query buffer. A single read can contain half a command or many commands (pipelining).
3. **Parse.** The RESP protocol is length-prefixed, so parsing is cheap: the array header tells Redis how many arguments follow and each bulk string states its own length. A request that is incomplete simply waits for more bytes. Because every argument has a length, values may contain any bytes, including newlines.
4. **Look up the command.** The name `HSET` is looked up in the command table (a dictionary). Redis checks the arity (number of arguments), that the client is authenticated, that the ACL user may run this command on these keys, and a few state checks: is the server out of memory (`maxmemory` with `noeviction`) while this is a write command, is this a read-only replica, is the client inside `MULTI`.
5. **Execute.** The command's C function runs. It finds the key in the keyspace dictionary, creates or updates the hash, and prepares the reply (here the integer `2`). It also notes side effects: mark the key as modified for `WATCH`, emit a keyspace notification if enabled, and tell the AOF and replication layers to log the command.
6. **Reply.** The reply bytes are appended to the client's output buffer. They are usually sent just before the loop sleeps again (`beforeSleep`), which batches replies from many clients into fewer system calls. Only if the socket cannot take everything does Redis register a writable event and finish later.
7. **Propagate.** The write is appended to the replication stream (and to the AOF buffer when AOF is on), so replicas and the log see the same commands in the same order.

Two details explain real behaviour. First, because step 6 batches replies, the average latency under load stays low even though the loop is shared. Second, step 7 happens at the end of the command, so replicas and the AOF see exactly the sequence the main thread executed; there is no concurrent interleaving to reason about.

### I/O threads

At high request rates the main thread spends a large share of its time not on your data but on system calls: reading bytes from sockets, parsing, and writing replies. **I/O threads** let helper threads do that part in parallel while the main thread keeps executing commands.

- Redis 6.0 introduced threaded I/O, mainly for writing replies, with an additional option for reads.
- Redis 8.0 reworked the I/O threading implementation as part of its performance work; the release notes describe large command-throughput and latency gains from many optimisations together. Treat the headline percentages as best-case vendor numbers measured on specific hardware and workloads, not as a promise for your system.
- The model is unchanged where it matters: **I/O threads never execute commands**. The main thread still runs each command, in order, alone.

You enable it with one directive:

blocks.code:
# Total number of threads used for I/O, counting the main thread.
# 1 (the default) means threading is off. Set it in redis.conf, then restart.
io-threads 4
blocks.title: redis.conf

blocks.text:
Guidance that holds across versions:

- Leave it at the default until you have measured. A typical single-node ShopStream cache serving a few tens of thousands of commands per second does not need it.
- Consider it when a single Redis process saturates one CPU core on network handling and you have spare cores. Set it clearly below the number of cores (the sample `redis.conf` suggests starting with `io-threads 4` only on machines with at least 4 cores).
- Verify the exact directive set for your version in its `redis.conf`; older releases also had `io-threads-do-reads`, and later versions changed how reads are threaded.
- If you are CPU-bound on command execution itself, I/O threads do not help. Scale out with replicas for reads or with Cluster for writes (see the Part on scaling).

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: More threads is not "multi-core Redis" A common misunderstanding is that `io-threads 8` makes Redis execute eight commands at once. It does not. Commands, Lua scripts and transactions remain strictly serialized on the main thread. If you want to use eight cores for data work, run several Redis processes, which is exactly what Redis Cluster does.

### Background threads and lazy free

Some jobs are too slow to run on the main thread, so Redis hands them to the bio threads:

- **Close file descriptors.** Closing a big file can block, for example when the kernel has to release its pages.
- **AOF fsync.** With `appendfsync everysec`, a background thread calls `fsync` once per second, so a slow disk does not stall commands (more on this in the AOF chapter).
- **Lazy free.** Deleting a key that holds a million elements means freeing a million small allocations. Done on the main thread, that is a visible pause. With lazy free the main thread unlinks the key from the keyspace in constant time and a background thread frees the memory.

You decide when to use lazy free in two ways. Explicitly, by choosing `UNLINK` instead of `DEL`, or `FLUSHALL ASYNC`/`FLUSHDB` `ASYNC` instead of the synchronous versions. Or by configuration, so even normal paths free in the background:

rows: A plain DEL behaves like UNLINK
FLUSHALL / FLUSHDB without a modifier behave as ASYNC
Keys removed by maxmemory eviction are freed in the background
Keys removed because their TTL elapsed are freed in the background
Implicit deletes, for example when SET or RENAME overwrites a big value
A replica flushes its old data asynchronously before a full sync

blocks.text:
*Lazy free directives. Defaults shown are those in the shipped redis.conf template; check your version.*

For big collections, make `UNLINK` your habit and consider turning on the lazy-free options if your values can get large. Freeing is not the only cost of big values, but it is the one that surprises people.

### Fork and copy-on-write, briefly

To produce an RDB snapshot without pausing clients, Redis calls `fork()`. The operating system gives the child a copy of the parent's memory *lazily*: both processes share the same physical pages until one of them writes. When the parent modifies a page after the fork, the kernel copies that page first (**copy-on-write**, COW) so the child keeps seeing the frozen snapshot.

Two costs follow, and both matter for latency:

- The `fork()` call itself must copy the page tables, which grows with dataset size. On a large instance this can block the main thread for tens or hundreds of milliseconds, and noticeably longer on some virtualised environments. `INFO` `stats` reports the last duration as `latest_fork_usec`.
- While the child runs, every first write to a shared page allocates a new page. In a write-heavy workload memory use can rise sharply, up to almost double in the worst case. Leave headroom in `maxmemory` and on the machine for this.

The persistence chapters later in this Part return to fork in detail. For now remember: the main thread is blocked only during the `fork()` call, not for the whole save.

### What this means for latency

The single-thread model gives Redis its simplicity and its sharpest edge. Latency of a command is its own execution time plus the time spent waiting behind the commands ahead of it.

Most commands take microseconds. The problem commands are those whose cost grows with the size of a collection or the size of the reply:

rows: Builds and sends one giant reply
`DEL on a key with millions` `of elements`
O(total size) work in one command
Store results, split the work, or compute elsewhere
Holds the loop for its whole run
O(N log N) work in the main thread
Pre-sorted structure such as a sorted set
blocks.caption: Commands that can block the loop on big data.

blocks.text: Two facts help you reason about cost. Complexity is documented on every command page as `O(1)`, `O(log N)`, `O(N)` and so on. And the slow log (`SLOWLOG GET`) records commands whose execution time exceeded `slowlog-log-slower-than` (default 10000 microseconds). It measures the execution step only, not waiting in the queue or network time, so a healthy slow log does not prove clients see low latency.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: One slow command is everyone's slow command If one worker issues `HGETALL` on a hash with two million fields and it takes 400 ms, then during those 400 ms the cart service, the session store and the rate limiter, all sharing that Redis, are frozen. The symptom in the application is a burst of timeouts across unrelated features. Find these commands with `SLOWLOG GET` and `INFO commandstats` and fix the data model; do not simply raise client timeouts.

A related queueing effect is client buffering. Each client has an input buffer (bounded by `client-query-buffer-limit`, 1 GB by default) and an output buffer. A slow consumer, for example a subscriber that does not read, makes its output buffer grow in Redis memory. Redis protects itself with `client-output-buffer-limit` rules per client class (normal, replica, pubsub) and will disconnect offenders. The chapter on pipelining and latency later in this Part covers this in context.

### Seeing it on a live server

You can observe the effects described here with a few commands. `INFO commandstats` shows, for each command, how often it ran and how much time it used in total, which is the quickest way to find the expensive one.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO commandstats
# Commandstats
cmdstat_set:calls=120000,usec=210000,usec_per_call=1.75,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
cmdstat_get:calls=980000,usec=1150000,usec_per_call=1.17,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
cmdstat_hgetall:calls=450,usec=9800000,usec_per_call=21777.78,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
blocks.title: Which commands consume the time?

blocks.text:
In this illustrative output `HGETALL` was called only 450 times but consumed more total time than a million `GET`s, at about 22 ms per call. That is the signature of a big-key problem. The command to inspect the cause is `MEMORY USAGE` (next chapter) or `redis-cli --bigkeys`.

### Connections, buffers and blocking commands

Several limits and behaviours around clients follow from the architecture.

- `maxclients` (default 10000) caps simultaneous connections. Redis also needs file descriptors for persistence files and replication, so it raises its own limit when it can; if the operating system limit is lower, Redis lowers `maxclients` and logs a warning. When the cap is hit new connections are refused with `ERR max number of clients reached`. A Spring service with a connection pool of 50 per instance and 40 instances already uses 2000 connections, so count before you scale out.
- `timeout` (default 0, never) closes idle clients after N seconds; `tcp-keepalive` (default 300 seconds) probes dead peers. Connection pools should validate or refresh connections rather than rely on the server to clean up.
- **Input and output buffers** belong to each client and live in Redis memory. The input buffer is limited by `client-query-buffer-limit`; output buffers by `client-output-buffer-limit`, with separate default rules for normal clients, replicas and pub/sub subscribers. A subscriber that stops reading is disconnected when its buffer passes the pub/sub limit.
- **Blocking commands** such as `BLPOP`, `BRPOP`, `XREAD BLOCK` and `WAIT` do *not* block the event loop. Redis parks that client in a table of blocked clients keyed by what it waits for, keeps serving everyone else, and wakes the client when the data arrives or the timeout elapses. That is why thousands of idle workers waiting on a queue cost almost nothing, whereas a thousand clients each running an expensive command would not.
- `MULTI`**/**`EXEC` **and Lua** run their commands back to back without yielding to the loop. This gives atomicity and also means a long transaction or script blocks everyone. The chapters on transactions and Lua scripting in this Part show how to keep them short.

### Experiment: feel the single thread

You can convince yourself of the one-command-at-a-time rule in two terminals. In the first, create a large set and ask for all of it; in the second, measure latency continuously with `redis-cli --latency`, which sends `PING` in a loop.

blocks.code:
$ seq 1 1000000 | sed 's/^/SADD big:set /' | redis-cli --pipe
$ redis-cli SMEMBERS big:set > /dev/null
blocks.title: Terminal 1: build a big set, then read all of it

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli --latency
min: 0, max: 1, avg: 0.11 (4521 samples)
min: 0, max: 118, avg: 0.62 (9714 samples)
blocks.title: Terminal 2: latency measured while terminal 1 runs the heavy command

blocks.text:
The numbers above are illustrative: the exact maximum depends on your machine, but the pattern is reliable. While the reply of a million elements is built and sent, the `PING` in terminal 2 waits in the queue and its measured latency jumps from a fraction of a millisecond to many milliseconds. Replace `SMEMBERS` with a loop of `SSCAN big:set <cursor>` `COUNT 1000` and the maximum falls back, because each call is tiny and other clients interleave between calls. That is the philosophy of the `SCAN` family: turn one long command into many short ones.

### Where the time goes in practice

For a typical small command such as `GET product:1001`, Redis spends a handful of microseconds on parsing and execution. The rest of what the client measures is the network round trip (tens to hundreds of microseconds in a data centre, milliseconds across zones) and the client library. Three consequences shape how you write code:

1. **Round trips dominate.** A loop of 100 sequential `GET`s costs 100 round trips. Pipelining (sending commands without waiting for each reply) or multi-key commands such as `MGET` cut that cost by an order of magnitude. See the chapter on pipelining later in this Part.
2. **The server is rarely the bottleneck for small commands.** A well-tuned single instance handles very high rates of simple operations on one core; before adding I/O threads, look at client concurrency and round trips.
3. **Tail latency matters more than the average.** One heavy command per second can leave the average untouched while the 99.9th percentile of every other client climbs. Watch percentiles, not means.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: If Redis is single-threaded, how can it handle so many clients, and can it use multiple cores? Redis runs commands on one thread, so no locking is needed and each command is atomic. It serves many connections by I/O multiplexing (`epoll`/`kqueue`): the single loop only touches sockets that are ready. Each command is fast because the data is in RAM and the structures are efficient. Since 6.0 optional I/O threads can parallelise socket reads and writes, and background threads handle fsync, file closing and lazy free, but command execution is still on one thread. To use more cores for data you run several instances: replicas for reads, Redis Cluster shards for writes.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Commands execute one at a time on the main thread, which makes every command atomic and removes the need for locks.
- The event loop (ae) multiplexes sockets with `epoll`/`kqueue`, and runs periodic work in `serverCron` at `hz` per second.
- A command goes through read, parse, look up, execute, reply and propagate; replies are batched before the loop sleeps.
- I/O threads (`io-threads`) speed up socket work only; background threads handle fsync, closing files and lazy free (`UNLINK`).
- `fork()` for RDB/AOF rewrite blocks briefly, and copy-on-write can raise memory use under heavy writes.
- Any O(N) command on a big collection delays every client; use `SCAN`-family commands, `UNLINK` and small keys.

Redis keeps the whole dataset in RAM, so memory is both its speed and its bill. The same logical hash can cost 100 bytes or 10 000 bytes depending on how Redis stores it internally, and the difference is the kind of thing that decides whether a cache fits on a 4 GB instance or needs a 16 GB one. This chapter explains how the keyspace is organised, which internal data structures back each Redis type, how to see which one you are using, and how to measure and reduce memory.

The central idea: a Redis type (string, list, hash, set, sorted set, stream) is a *contract*, not a data structure. Behind the contract Redis picks an **encoding**, an actual in-memory representation, and switches encodings as a value grows. Small values get compact, cache-friendly encodings; large values get structures with better asymptotic complexity.

### The keyspace is one big hash table

Every database (the numbered ones, 0 to 15) is a dictionary from key to value. The dictionary is a classic hash table with chaining: an array of buckets, each bucket a short linked list of entries. Looking up `product:1001` hashes the key name, picks a bucket, and compares keys along the chain. That is O(1) on average.

When the table gets too full, it must grow (about doubling). Copying all entries at once would freeze the server, so Redis does **incremental rehashing**: it allocates the new, larger table, keeps both, and moves a few buckets on every dictionary operation and in `serverCron` (the `activerehashing yes` setting lets cron help). During the move, lookups check both tables. Two practical consequences:

- During rehashing of a huge dictionary, memory briefly holds two bucket arrays (just the pointer arrays, not the values).
- Growing is smooth in latency terms, but the array allocation itself is a large block of memory, which is one reason an instance with 100 million keys needs headroom.

Each entry in the keyspace carries a **redisObject**: a small header (16 bytes on 64-bit builds) storing the type, the encoding, an LRU/LFU field used for eviction, a reference count, and a pointer to the actual data. That header, the key string, and the dictionary entry are the fixed per-key overhead, typically several dozen bytes before any of your data. Keep that in mind when you consider storing 50 million tiny values as separate keys.

### Strings: SDS and three encodings

Redis does not use C strings. It uses **SDS** (Simple Dynamic Strings): a small header with the current length and allocated capacity, followed by the bytes. This gives O(1) length, safe appending (spare capacity avoids repeated reallocation), and binary safety (a value may contain zero bytes, since length is stored rather than found by scanning for a terminator).

A string value is stored in one of three encodings, which you can see with `OBJECT ENCODING`:

- `int`: the value is a number that fits in a 64-bit signed integer. Redis stores the number directly in the object's pointer field, with no separate allocation. This is why counters are cheap.
- `embstr`: a short string (44 bytes or less on the usual 64-bit build) stored in the *same* memory block as its redisObject. One allocation, good cache locality. Embedded strings are read-only; modifying one converts it.
- `raw`: longer strings, or any string that has been modified in place (`APPEND`, `SETRANGE`), get a separate SDS allocation.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET views 100
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING views
"int"
127.0.0.1:6379> SET sku:1 "abc"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING sku:1
"embstr"
127.0.0.1:6379> APPEND sku:1 x
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING sku:1
"raw"
blocks.title: The three string encodings

blocks.text:
The practical lesson: a string you only `SET` and `GET` is cheaper than one you keep mutating with `APPEND`. For counters use `INCR` on integers rather than storing numbers as text you edit yourself.

### Compact encodings for small collections

For small hashes, sorted sets, sets and lists, a pointer-heavy structure (hash table, skip list, linked list) wastes memory: each element needs its own allocation plus pointers, and jemalloc rounds every allocation up to a size class. Redis therefore stores small collections in a **listpack**, and switches to the big structure when a limit is crossed.

#### Listpack

A **listpack** is a single contiguous block of bytes holding a sequence of entries, each encoded with a small header and its own length so you can walk forward and backward. There are no pointers between entries and just one allocation for the whole collection. Integers are stored in 1 to 9 bytes depending on magnitude, strings with a length prefix.

**A hash with three fields in listpack encoding (conceptual layout)**

The trade-off is plain: lookup in a listpack is a linear scan, O(N), and inserting in the middle may move bytes. That is a fine bargain when N is small (the scan touches one or two cache lines) and a bad one when N is large. Hence the thresholds below. Listpack replaced the older **ziplist** in Redis 7.0; ziplist could trigger a "cascading update" when one entry's size change forced its neighbours' length headers to grow, and listpack was designed to avoid that.

#### Intset

A set whose members are all integers fits in an **intset**: a sorted array of integers of the smallest width (16, 32 or 64 bit) that holds all of them. Membership is a binary search, O(log N). Add one non-integer member, or exceed `set-max-intset-entries`, and it converts to a hash table. Newer versions also allow small sets of non-integers to use a listpack (the directive is `set-max-listpack-entries`); check your version's `redis.conf`.

#### Quicklist

Lists can be long, and a single listpack would make pushes at the head costly. A **quicklist** is a doubly linked list whose nodes are listpacks. Pushing and popping at either end is O(1), and the per-node packing keeps pointer overhead low. `list-max-listpack-size` controls node size: a positive number limits entries per node, a negative number limits bytes (`-2`, the default, means 8 KB per node). `list-compress-depth` can LZF-compress the middle nodes of very long lists, keeping the nodes near both ends uncompressed because those are the hot ones. A very short list is stored as one plain listpack.

#### Hash table

The big encoding for hashes and sets is the same kind of dictionary as the keyspace: O(1) average access, but each entry costs allocations and pointers, which is where the memory goes.

#### Skiplist

Sorted sets that outgrow their limits use a **skiplist** plus a hash table. The skiplist is a linked list with extra "express lanes" of random heights, so a search can skip ahead and find any element by score in O(log N); it also supports range queries by walking the bottom level. The companion dictionary maps member to score so `ZSCORE` is O(1). The two structures share the member strings. This is why `ZADD` is O(log N) while `ZSCORE` is O(1).

**Skiplist idea: higher levels skip further**

#### Radix tree for streams

A stream is a **radix tree** (rax) keyed by entry ID. Each leaf holds a *macro node*: a listpack containing many entries, with field names stored once per node and repeated entries compressed as deltas. `stream-node-max-bytes` (default 4096) and `stream-node-max-entries` (default 100) bound a node. This makes appending and range-reading by ID fast and compact. Consumer groups add their own rax of pending entries (the PEL), covered in the chapter on streams.

### Which encoding do I have, and when does it change?

The table lists the encodings you can see with `OBJECT ENCODING`, and the default thresholds that trigger a change. Defaults below were confirmed against a Redis 7.0 server and the 8.0 configuration template. They can change between versions, so read them from your own server with `CONFIG GET`.

rows: not an integer; length above 44 bytes; modified in place
more fields or longer values than limits
non-integer member, or too many members
more members or longer members than limits
always a radix tree of listpacks
blocks.caption: Types, encodings and the config that switches them.

blocks.text:
Hashes with per-field expiration (`HEXPIRE`, Redis 7.4 and later) use listpack and hashtable variants that also store the expiry times; depending on version you may see an encoding name such as `listpackex` for them. That is the same idea with an extra column.

You can watch a conversion happen. Here a hash starts as a listpack and becomes a hashtable once a value is longer than `hash-max-listpack-value`:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET product:1001 name "Mug" price 1299 stock 40
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING product:1001
"listpack"
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET product:1001 description \
  "Hand-glazed ceramic mug, 350 ml, dishwasher and microwave safe, six colours"
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING product:1001
"hashtable"
blocks.title: Encoding conversion by value length

blocks.text: A product description pushing the whole hash over the 64-byte value limit is a realistic ShopStream accident: one long field makes *all* the fields of that product use the memory-hungry encoding. If most of your hashes are small except one fat field, consider keeping the long text in its own key.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Conversions are one-way Redis converts a collection to the large encoding when a threshold is crossed, but does not convert it back when elements are removed (a rebuild such as `RESTORE`, a restart that reloads from RDB, or copying into a new key can produce the compact form again). Never rely on a particular encoding in application logic; use it only for diagnosis.

### Measuring memory

Three tools cover most needs.

`MEMORY USAGE key [SAMPLES n]` returns the bytes a key costs, including its key name and internal overhead. For nested values it samples some elements and extrapolates (default 5 samples; pass `SAMPLES 0` for an exact walk, which costs more CPU).

`INFO memory` gives the instance view. The fields to know are `used_memory` (what Redis asked the allocator for), `used_memory_rss` (what the operating system reports resident), `used_memory_peak`, `used_memory_dataset` versus `used_memory_overhead`, and `mem_fragmentation_ratio`.

`MEMORY STATS` and `MEMORY DOCTOR` give a breakdown and plain-language hints.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET product:1 name "Mug" price 1299 stock 40
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY USAGE product:1
(integer) 96
127.0.0.1:6379> SET product:1:name "Mug"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY USAGE product:1:name
(integer) 72
127.0.0.1:6379> SET product:1:price 1299
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY USAGE product:1:price
(integer) 56
blocks.title: Cost of a small product, as a hash versus separate string keys

blocks.text:
These byte counts come from a test on Redis 7.0; yours will differ by version and key length, but the shape is stable. The one hash costs about as much as one or two of the three separate keys, so the three-key layout is roughly twice as large (and needs three lookups and three TTLs). Small objects as hashes in listpack encoding are the most memory-efficient way to store records.

#### Fragmentation and the allocator

Redis uses **jemalloc** by default on Linux. Allocators serve requests from size classes, so some bytes inside each block are wasted (internal fragmentation) and freed memory can be scattered in pieces too small to reuse (external fragmentation). The ratio `mem_fragmentation_ratio` is `used_memory_rss / used_memory`.

- Around 1.0 to 1.5 on a busy instance: normal.
- Much above 1.5: memory is resident but not in use. Typical causes are a large delete (or expiry wave) followed by new keys of different sizes, or a freshly started tiny instance (the ratio is meaningless when `used_memory` is a few megabytes).
- Below 1.0: the operating system has swapped part of Redis to disk. This is an emergency; latency will collapse.

If fragmentation is real and large, options are to restart through a replica failover, or to enable **active** **defragmentation** (`activedefrag yes`), which compacts memory in the background with bounded CPU (`active-defrag-cycle-min`/`max`). It is supported with the bundled jemalloc and is off by default.

### Reducing memory: what actually works

1. **Use the right structure.** Small records as hashes (listpack) beat one key per field. Counters as integers. IDs as integers in sets (intset).
2. **Shorten keys and values where it matters.** A key like `shopstream:production:catalog:product:1001:name` repeats 40 bytes for every entry. Keep names readable, but do not be verbose at 50 million keys. Compress large JSON on the client when CPU is cheaper than RAM.
3. **Use expiry.** Data that should not live forever must have a TTL (next chapter).
4. **Avoid huge keys.** One key with 20 million elements is hard to delete, hard to migrate in a cluster, and spikes latency; split by bucket (for example `cart:{userId}` instead of a single `carts` hash).
5. **Tune thresholds with care.** Raising `hash-max-listpack-entries` keeps bigger hashes compact but makes every access scan more bytes. Measure with `MEMORY USAGE` and `redis-benchmark` before changing it in production.
6. **Upgrade.** Recent releases reduce memory by themselves. The 8.0 notes cite memory savings on replicas, and the 8.6 notes say hash and sorted-set operations use unified field/value and score/value structures, delivering a "substantial memory reduction". The notes give no fixed percentages for 8.6, so benchmark your own data.

### A worked estimate: the ShopStream catalogue

Suppose ShopStream has 200 000 products and the catalogue cache keeps each as ten short fields, around 400 bytes of payload. Compare three layouts.

#### Layout A: one hash per product (listpack)

Each hash stays under 512 entries and every value under 64 bytes, so it is a listpack. Cost per product is roughly the payload plus a key name (`product:100000`, 14 bytes), the dictionary entry and redisObject (several dozen bytes), and allocator rounding. A planning figure is 500 to 600 bytes per product, so 200 000 products need about 100 to 120 MB. This is an estimate for planning, not a measurement; sample real data with `MEMORY USAGE` before you trust it.

#### Layout B: ten string keys per product

Now there are 2 000 000 keys. Each carries its own dictionary entry, redisObject and key string, and a long key name such as `product:100000:description`. The overhead per key is commonly 50 to 70 bytes plus rounding, so overhead alone is 100 to 140 MB before any payload, and every product needs ten lookups and ten TTLs. It is typically at least double the size of layout A.

#### Layout C: one JSON string per product

A serialised JSON document in a single string key uses one key and one value. It is compact when you always read the whole object, but you cannot change one field without rewriting everything. The Redis JSON type (covered in the data structures Part) keeps the document in a native binary tree and allows path updates, with its own overhead.

The choice depends on access pattern more than size. If the application nearly always reads the full product, a single value (hash or JSON string) wins. If it frequently updates a single field such as `stock`, a hash is the natural fit.

### Bucketing: a classic memory trick

Because small hashes are so compact, there is an old technique for storing a very large number of tiny values: split the key space into buckets. Instead of 50 million keys `user:avatar:{id}`, store them as fields in hashes whose name comes from the id divided by a fixed number.

blocks.code:
# user id 123456789 -> bucket = id / 500 = 246913, field = id % 500 = 289
HSET avatar:246913 289 "u/ab12.png"
HGET avatar:246913 289
blocks.title: Instead of one key per user, one hash per 500 users

blocks.text:
With a bucket size that keeps each hash within `hash-max-listpack-entries`, every bucket remains a listpack, saving the per-key overhead. The costs are real: you cannot give an individual field a key-level TTL (per-field TTL from 7.4 softens this), keys are harder to inspect, and hot buckets in a cluster can unbalance shards. Use it only when you have measured that key overhead dominates, typically beyond tens of millions of tiny entries.

### Finding the big and the wasteful

Two redis-cli scans help find outliers. Both use `SCAN` internally, so they are safe on a live server, but they add load, so run them off peak or against a replica.

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli --bigkeys
[00.00%] Biggest string found so far '"session:abc123"' with 212 bytes
[00.00%] Biggest hash   found so far '"product:1001"' with 9 fields
[28.57%] Biggest zset   found so far '"lb:bestsellers:daily"' with 51234 members
-------- summary -------
Sampled 8402 keys in the keyspace!
Total key length in bytes is 129344 (avg len 15.39)
Biggest   hash found '"product:1001"' has 9 fields
Biggest   zset found '"lb:bestsellers:daily"' has 51234 members
blocks.title: Find the biggest key of each type (shortened, illustrative)

blocks.text: `--bigkeys` counts elements; `--memkeys` reports bytes using `MEMORY USAGE`. Redis 8.6 adds a `HOTKEYS` command for finding the keys that receive the most traffic, which is a different problem from keys that use the most memory.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Memory counted by maxmemory is not the whole process `maxmemory` limits roughly the memory Redis uses for data. Output buffers for replicas, the replication backlog and AOF buffers are not counted toward eviction decisions the same way, and a fork for a snapshot may double memory under heavy writes. Setting `maxmemory` to 100% of the machine's RAM invites the out-of-memory killer. A common starting rule is to leave 25 to 50 percent of RAM free when persistence is on; the operations Part gives more precise sizing advice.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why does Redis store small hashes as a listpack, and what is the downside? A listpack is one contiguous allocation with no per-element pointers, so it is far smaller and cache friendly than a hash table with a node per field. The downside is O(N) lookup. That is acceptable only while N is small, so Redis converts to a real hash table once the entry count or value size crosses `hash-max-listpack-entries` or `hash-max-listpack-value`. Same pattern for sorted sets (listpack to skiplist), lists (quicklist of listpacks) and sets (intset to hash table).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A type is a contract; the encoding (`OBJECT ENCODING`) is the representation and changes with size.
- Small collections use listpack or intset; large ones use hashtable, skiplist or quicklist. Thresholds are configurable and conversion is one-way.
- Per-key overhead is real (dictionary entry, redisObject, key string); many tiny keys cost far more than a few small hashes.
- Measure with `MEMORY USAGE`, `INFO memory` and `MEMORY STATS`; read `mem_fragmentation_ratio` with the context above.
- Reduce memory by choosing structures, bucketing, TTLs, shorter keys and upgrading; leave RAM headroom beyond `maxmemory`.

A cache without expiry slowly turns into a second copy of your database that is always a little wrong. Sessions that never expire fill memory with logged-out users. Redis solves both with a **time to live** (TTL): you attach a deadline to a key and Redis deletes the key when the deadline passes. This chapter shows the commands, then explains how Redis actually enforces them (it is more subtle than "a timer per key") and how expiry interacts with replicas, the AOF and hashes.

### Setting, reading and removing a TTL

A TTL belongs to the *key*, not the value. Most keys have none and live until deleted or evicted. The relevant commands:

-1 = key exists but has no TTL, -2 = key does not exist
Returns 1 if a TTL was removed
`SET key v EX s / PX ms /` `EXAT ts / PXAT ts`

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:abc123 "user:42" EX 1800
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL session:abc123
(integer) 1800
127.0.0.1:6379> GETEX session:abc123 EX 1800
"user:42"
127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE session:abc123 100 GT
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> PERSIST session:abc123
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL session:abc123
(integer) -1
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL no:such:key
(integer) -2
blocks.title: Working with TTLs on a ShopStream session

blocks.text:
Three behaviours catch people out:

- **Overwriting clears the TTL.** A plain `SET key newvalue` removes any existing expiry. If you refresh a cached product with `SET product:1001 json` and forget `EX`, the key becomes immortal. Use `SET ... EX` every time, or `KEEPTTL` if you really want to keep the old deadline.
- **Other commands keep it.** `INCR`, `APPEND`, `HSET`, `LPUSH` and similar modify the value and leave the TTL alone. `RENAME` moves the TTL to the new name. `DEL` removes the key and its TTL.
- **A past deadline deletes immediately.** `EXPIRE key 0`, `EXPIRE key -1`, or `EXPIREAT` with a timestamp in the past removes the key right away.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Keep the TTL atomic with the write `SET key value EX 60` is one command. `SET key value` followed by `EXPIRE key 60` is two; if the client crashes between them the key lives forever. The same reasoning is why `SETEX`, `PSETEX` and `SETNX` are legacy: the `SET` options cover them.

### How Redis expires keys: lazy plus active

Redis stores a deadline per key in a second dictionary (the *expires* dictionary), a mapping from key to absolute millisecond timestamp. It would be too expensive to keep every deadline in a sorted structure and wake up exactly on time. Instead, Redis combines two cheap strategies.

**Passive (lazy) expiration.** Every time a command touches a key, Redis first checks the key's deadline. If it has passed, the key is deleted on the spot and the command sees "no such key". So a read never returns a logically expired value. This costs nothing for keys no one accesses, which is exactly the problem: an expired key that nobody asks for would sit in memory forever.

**Active expiration.** To reclaim those, Redis runs an *active expire cycle* many times per second, inside `serverCron` (and a short "fast" cycle before the loop sleeps). The classic algorithm, which is still the basis today:

1. Pick 20 random keys from the set of keys that have a TTL.
2. Delete every one of them that has expired.
3. If more than 25 percent of the sample was expired, go back to step 1.

The loop is time-bounded, by default to a small slice of CPU per second, so expiry can never take over the server. The directive `active-expire-effort` (1 to 10, default 1) lets you trade CPU for more aggressive cleanup if expired keys pile up.

**Why 25 percent? A feedback loop that scales with the garbage**

blocks.code:
sample 20 keys with TTL ──▶ delete expired ones
        │
        ├─ expired ≤ 25% of sample  ──▶ stop; few dead keys, check again next tick
        │
        └─ expired > 25% of sample  ──▶ sample again (likely lots of dead keys left)

blocks.text:
What follows from this design:

- **Expired keys can still use memory for a while.** After a mass expiry (for example thousands of sessions created in the same minute with the same TTL), the sampling cycle may take several seconds to clear them. `INFO stats` shows `expired_keys` (a running count) and `expired_stale_perc` indicates how stale the TTL set currently is.
- **Mass expiry at the same instant is a latency risk.** If a million keys expire in the same second, the active cycle can spend its full time budget repeatedly, and the main thread has less time for clients. Add random jitter to TTLs in caches (the caching patterns Part uses 10 to 20 percent jitter).
- **Lazy free applies.** With `lazyfree-lazy-expire yes` the memory of expired keys is released on a background thread.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: TTL does not mean "memory freed at that instant" `DBSIZE` and `INFO keyspace` count keys that are logically expired but not yet deleted. Do not size capacity from the number of keys you expect to be alive at a moment; look at `used_memory`.

### Expiry with replicas, AOF and RDB

Expiry has to give the same result on every node, but clocks differ and replicas receive commands later. Redis therefore keeps one rule: **only the primary decides that a key has expired.**

- When the primary deletes an expired key (lazily or actively), it sends a `DEL` (or `UNLINK` with lazy free) to its replicas and appends it to the AOF. Replicas do not delete keys on their own clock.
- A replica still hides keys that are logically expired for *reads*: a `GET` on a replica returns nil for a key whose deadline has passed, even before the `DEL` arrives. Memory is freed only when the `DEL` comes.
- In the AOF, relative commands such as `EXPIRE key 100` are rewritten as absolute `PEXPIREAT` commands, so replaying the AOF later does not extend lifetimes. Likewise `SET ... EX 60` is propagated with an absolute deadline.
- An RDB file stores absolute expiry timestamps. When a primary loads an RDB it skips keys that have already expired; a replica loads them and waits for `DEL` from the primary. If the server was stopped for an hour, all keys with a TTL shorter than an hour are gone on restart.
- Inside a Lua script or `MULTI`, time is effectively frozen to the start of the script, so a key does not expire half way through; scripts see a consistent clock.

This means a primary and replica with badly skewed clocks can behave oddly with absolute timestamps (`EXPIREAT`). Run NTP on all nodes.

### Expiry on hash fields

Before Redis 7.4 a TTL applied only to a whole key, which made "one hash per user with some fields expiring early" impossible. Now fields can have their own TTL: `HEXPIRE`, `HPEXPIRE`, `HEXPIREAT`, `HPEXPIREAT`, `HTTL`, `HPTTL`, `HEXPIRETIME`, `HPERSIST`. Redis 8.0 added `HGETEX` (read and set field TTL), `HSETEX` (write and set TTL) and `HGETDEL` (read and delete). Field commands take a `FIELDS numfields field [field ...]` clause and return one status per field.

blocks.code:
HSET product:1001 name "Mug" price 1299 flash_price 999
HEXPIRE product:1001 3600 FIELDS 1 flash_price
HTTL product:1001 FIELDS 2 flash_price name
blocks.title: Per-field TTL on a ShopStream product hash (syntax from the 7.4+ command pages)

blocks.text:
The `HTTL` reply for that call is a list with the remaining seconds for `flash_price` and `-1` for `name` (the field exists with no TTL); `-2` means the field does not exist. When the last field of a hash expires the key itself is removed. Field expiry is also implemented with a passive part and an active part, but it is tracked separately from key-level expiry, so a key can have its own TTL and also fields with TTLs. Use it for things like a flash-sale price or a "verified" flag that must lapse; do not use it as a substitute for a separate key when you need keyspace notifications per item.

### Patterns: session expiry in a ShopStream service

Two designs for sessions show why the TTL commands have so many options.

- **Absolute expiry**: the session ends a fixed time after login no matter what. Set the TTL once with `SET ... EX` and never refresh it. Use `EXPIRE ... NX` when you re-save the session and must not extend it.
- **Sliding expiry**: the session lives as long as the user stays active. Refresh the TTL on every request with `GETEX key` `EX seconds` (read and refresh in one round trip), or `EXPIRE key seconds`. Combine with `EXPIRE ... LT` or `GT` if you need to enforce a rule such as "never shorten" or "never exceed a cap".

A practical combination is a sliding 30-minute idle timeout with an absolute 12-hour maximum: store the login time in the session, refresh the idle TTL on each request, and refuse to refresh once the absolute limit passed. Here it is with the Spring `StringRedisTemplate`:

blocks.title: SessionStore.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: `set(key, value, Duration)` maps to a single `SET ... PX` (or `EX`) command, so there is no window with a TTL-less key, and `getAndExpire` maps to `GETEX`. Never write `set(key, value)` followed by `expire(key, ...)` in two calls.

### TTL jitter and keyspace notifications

If you load 100 000 products at start-up with the same 10-minute TTL, they all expire in the same few seconds, the cache goes cold at once, and the database sees a burst of misses (a cache avalanche, covered in the caching failures chapter). Add random jitter when you set the TTL:

blocks.title: TtlJitter.java

blocks.text: Redis can also publish an event when a key expires, using **keyspace notifications**. They are off by default (`notify-keyspace-events ""`) because they cost CPU. To receive `expired` events set `notify-keyspace-events Ex` (`E` selects keyevent channels, `x` the expired events) and subscribe to `__keyevent@0__:expired`. The events are emitted at the moment Redis actually deletes the key, not the instant the TTL elapsed, and because they travel through pub/sub nobody who was disconnected receives them.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not build workflows on expiry notifications Keyspace notifications with the `expired` event fire when Redis *deletes* the key, which may be seconds after the deadline, and are delivered by fire-and-forget pub/sub, so they can be lost. The chapter on delayed tasks in the Patterns Part shows a safer design with a sorted set.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How does Redis expire keys, and why can an expired key still be in memory? Two mechanisms. Lazy expiration checks the deadline whenever a key is accessed and deletes it if it is past due. Active expiration repeatedly samples 20 random keys that have a TTL, deletes the expired ones, and repeats if more than 25 percent were expired, within a CPU time budget. Keys that are never touched and not yet sampled stay in memory until a sample finds them. Replicas do not expire on their own; the primary sends `DEL` for each expired key.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A TTL is per key; `SET` without `EX`/`KEEPTTL` clears it, so set value and TTL in one command.
- Expiry = lazy check on access + active random sampling (20 keys, repeat while over 25 percent are expired).
- Expired keys can linger in memory, and synchronized TTLs can cause latency bumps: add jitter.
- Only the primary expires keys; replicas and the AOF receive explicit deletes and absolute timestamps.
- Hash fields can have their own TTL since 7.4 (`HEXPIRE`), and 8.0 added `HGETEX`/`HSETEX`/`HGETDEL`.

Expiry removes data you declared temporary. **Eviction** removes data when Redis runs out of the memory you allowed it, even though you never said the data was disposable. It is what lets Redis serve as a cache: a full cache keeps working by dropping the least valuable entries to make room for new ones.

### maxmemory and what happens when it is reached

Set a ceiling with `maxmemory` (bytes, or with suffixes like `2gb`). The default `0` means no limit on 64-bit systems, so Redis will grow until the operating system kills it. Always set a limit in production, below physical RAM with room for fork copy-on-write, buffers and the OS.

When a command that may add data arrives and memory use is above the limit, Redis tries to free memory according to `maxmemory-policy`. If it cannot (or the policy is `noeviction`), commands that would increase memory are rejected with an error, while reads and deletes still work.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET maxmemory 2mb
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy
1) "maxmemory-policy"
2) "noeviction"
127.0.0.1:6379> SET product:99999 "x"
(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.
127.0.0.1:6379> GET product:1001
"{...cached json...}"
blocks.title: The default policy refuses writes at the limit

blocks.text:
An application that gets `OOM command not allowed` from Redis usually surfaces it as a 500. For a cache this is the wrong default. For a primary datastore (queues, locks you cannot lose) it is the right one, because silently deleting data would be worse.

### The eviction policies

rows: Does not evict; writes that need memory fail
blocks.caption: maxmemory-policy values.

blocks.text:
The `volatile-*` policies only consider keys that have an expiry; if none do, they behave like `noeviction`. That makes them a trap: a cache whose writers forgot `EX` will start failing writes even though it is "full of cache data".

**LRM** (least recently modified), new in 8.6, orders by the last time a key was *written* rather than read. The release notes describe it as giving better control for write-heavy workloads; it suits data where being read often does not prove it is valuable, but being updated recently does. If you run an older server, the `CONFIG SET` for these policy names fails with an error that lists the policies your version accepts.

### Approximated LRU and LFU

True LRU needs a linked list updated on every access: extra pointers per key and extra work per read. Redis approximates instead. Each key's redisObject holds a 24-bit field with a coarse last-access clock. To evict, Redis **samples** `maxmemory-samples` random keys (default 5), compares them, and evicts the best victim. Since version 3.0 it also keeps a small pool of good candidates between rounds, which improves accuracy. Raising `maxmemory-samples` to 10 gets close to true LRU at a modest CPU cost; lowering it saves CPU.

**LFU** uses the same 24 bits differently: 16 bits for the time of the last decrement and 8 bits for a logarithmic access counter (a Morris counter). The counter grows probabilistically, so it saturates only after a very large number of accesses:

- `lfu-log-factor` (default 10): higher means the counter grows more slowly. With 10, it saturates around one million accesses.
- `lfu-decay-time` (default 1): minutes without access before the counter drops by one. `0` disables decay.

LFU protects keys that are *consistently* popular from being flushed by a one-time scan of many rarely used keys, which pure LRU would let through. You can see the counter with `OBJECT FREQ` (only when an LFU policy is selected; otherwise Redis answers with an error).

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET hot 1
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT FREQ hot
(integer) 5
127.0.0.1:6379> GET hot
"1"
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT FREQ hot
(integer) 6

### Eviction is work on the main thread

Eviction happens before a command is executed: Redis checks memory, evicts until it is under the limit, then runs the command. A single big write may need to evict many keys, and freeing a large value takes time. Two knobs help:

- `maxmemory-eviction-tenacity` (default 10) bounds how long a single eviction round may run; higher values evict more aggressively per call, lower values protect latency but let memory overshoot temporarily.
- `lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes` frees evicted values on a background thread.

Replicas ignore `maxmemory` by default (`replica-ignore-maxmemory yes`): the primary evicts and sends `DEL` for evicted keys to replicas, so replicas stay identical. Memory used by replication output buffers and AOF buffers is not meant to count toward the `maxmemory` data limit, so leave spare RAM for them.

### A worked scenario: sizing the catalogue cache

ShopStream's catalogue has 200 000 products at roughly 600 bytes each in Redis, about 120 MB for all of them, but the traffic is skewed: 5 percent of products receive most of the page views. The team sets `maxmemory 100mb` on a cache instance with `allkeys-lfu`. What happens?

1. The first misses fill the cache with hot and cold products alike until memory reaches 100 MB (about 83 percent of the whole catalogue).
2. A new write now triggers eviction: Redis samples keys and removes the one with the lowest LFU counter. Hot products have high counters (they are read constantly) and survive; a product seen once has a low counter and goes first.
3. The hit ratio stays high because the working set (the hot 5 percent, around 6 MB) fits comfortably. `evicted_keys` ticks up slowly; that is the cache doing its job, not an incident.

Now imagine a nightly report job that scans every product exactly once. Under `allkeys-lru` that scan makes every product look "recently used" and can push out the genuinely hot keys. Under `allkeys-lfu` the scan produces counters of 1 and the hot keys stay protected, which is why LFU is the better default for catalogue-style data. It is not free: LFU needs a few accesses to learn that a new key is valuable, and a key that was hot yesterday decays slowly (`lfu-decay-time`).

You can reproduce the basic behaviour on a laptop. With `maxmemory 2mb` and `allkeys-lru`, writing 30 000 keys of 100 bytes succeeds for every command, and `INFO stats` afterwards shows tens of thousands of `evicted_keys` while `DBSIZE` stays near what fits in memory:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> DBSIZE
(integer) 5810
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO stats
# Stats
evicted_keys:30494
blocks.title: Writes keep succeeding, old keys disappear (typical output)

blocks.text:
The `DBSIZE` and `evicted_keys` values are from a test on a 2 MB limit, so they will differ on your machine. The point is the pair: the dataset size is capped, and evictions counted instead of errors.

### Choosing a policy

rows: Pure cache; every key can be rebuilt; all have TTLs or not
allkeys-lru, or allkeys-lfu if some keys are hot for long periods (product pages) and you fear scan pollution
Cache and durable data in the same instance (not recommended)
volatile-lru or volatile-lfu, and set TTLs only on the cache keys
Redis as primary store, queues, streams, locks
noeviction; plan capacity and monitor memory instead
Write-heavy data where recent writes matter (8.6+)
Strict ordering by deadline (for example short-lived tokens)
allkeys-random is cheap and often adequate
blocks.caption: Which policy for which job.

blocks.text:
The cleanest design for a ShopStream deployment is to separate roles. The catalogue cache runs on an instance with `allkeys-lfu`; sessions, carts and the order stream run on another with `noeviction` and persistence. Mixing both on one instance forces compromises in both directions.

#### Monitoring eviction

Watch `evicted_keys` in `INFO stats`, `used_memory` against `maxmemory`, and the cache hit ratio from `keyspace_hits` and `keyspace_misses`. A steadily rising `evicted_keys` with a falling hit ratio means the cache is too small for its working set. If evicted keys include things you expected to be permanent (sessions), your policy or your separation of roles is wrong.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Evicting queue data is data loss With any `allkeys-*` policy a list or stream used as a job queue is a candidate for eviction like any other key. One memory spike and the whole queue key can vanish, with no error. Keep queues and locks on a `noeviction` instance, or use `volatile-*` policies and never set a TTL on them.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What happens when Redis reaches maxmemory, and how does it choose what to evict? With the default `noeviction`, write commands that need memory fail with an OOM error. With any other policy Redis evicts keys before executing the command: it samples `maxmemory-samples` keys (default 5) from all keys or only from keys with a TTL, depending on the policy, and removes the one that is least recently used, least frequently used, random, nearest to expiry (or least recently modified, in 8.6). LRU and LFU are approximations built from a per-key 24-bit field, avoiding the cost of exact bookkeeping.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Always set `maxmemory`; the default of 0 lets Redis grow until the OS intervenes.
- `noeviction` rejects writes (reads still work); the other policies evict by LRU, LFU, random, TTL or (8.6) LRM, over all keys or only keys with a TTL.
- LRU and LFU are sampled approximations; `maxmemory-samples` trades accuracy for CPU.
- `volatile-*` policies do nothing for keys without TTL, so a cache without TTLs can still hit OOM.
- Do not put queues, locks or sessions you cannot lose on an instance that evicts; separate cache from durable roles.

Everything we have discussed so far lives in RAM, and RAM is erased when the process stops. If Redis only ever held disposable cache data that would be fine, but sessions, carts, and order events must survive a restart. Redis offers two persistence mechanisms, which can be used alone or together: **RDB snapshots** (this chapter) and the **append-only** **file** (next chapter). The question to keep in mind for both is: *if the server dies right now, how much do I lose, and how* *long does the restart take?*

### The idea: a point-in-time photograph

An RDB (Redis DataBase) file is a compact, binary dump of the entire dataset at one moment. Redis writes it to a file called `dump.rdb` (the default name). On restart, Redis reads that file back into memory. Think of it as a photograph of the dataset: small, fast to load, and perfect for backups, but anything that changed after the photo was taken is not in it.

The main trigger is configuration. Rules of the form `save <seconds> <changes>` mean: take a snapshot if at least `<changes>` write operations happened in the last `<seconds>`. The commonly shipped default (Redis 7.x and later templates) is:

blocks.code:
# Snapshot if: 3600s and >=1 change, or 300s and >=100 changes, or 60s and >=10000 changes
save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000
dbfilename dump.rdb
dir /data
blocks.title: redis.conf

blocks.text:
This rule set bounds data loss in a crash to minutes in quiet periods and still saves quickly under heavy writes. `save ""` disables snapshots entirely. You can also trigger one by hand:

- `BGSAVE` forks a child process and returns immediately. This is what you want.
- `SAVE` writes the snapshot **on the main thread** and blocks all clients until it finishes. Use it only in a maintenance window or tests.

Redis also snapshots on a clean shutdown (`SHUTDOWN`, or SIGTERM) if any save rule is configured, and a primary does a `BGSAVE`-style dump when a replica needs a full resynchronization (see the Part on replication).

### How BGSAVE works: fork and copy-on-write

The trick that makes snapshots cheap is `fork()` plus **copy-on-write** (COW), introduced in the server architecture chapter. Here is the full sequence.

**BGSAVE timeline**

blocks.code:
parent (serves clients)                          child (snapshot writer)
───────────────────────                          ───────────────────────
BGSAVE received
fork() ────────────────────────────────────────▶ starts; sees memory as of fork time
(main thread blocked only for the fork call)
keeps executing commands                         iterates the dataset, serialises
  first write to a memory page ─▶ kernel copies    to temp-<pid>.rdb, compresses,
  that page for the parent (COW)                   fsyncs incrementally
...                                              finishes, rename(temp-<pid>.rdb → dump.rdb)
notices child exit, updates INFO ◀───────────── exits

blocks.text:
Points to notice:

1. **The snapshot is consistent** because the child sees frozen memory. It does not matter that the parent keeps changing data.
2. **The file is replaced atomically.** The child writes to a temporary file and renames it over `dump.rdb` at the end, so a crash during the save leaves the previous good snapshot in place.
3. **Memory can grow during the save.** Each page the parent modifies is duplicated. A mostly-read workload adds little; a workload that touches many keys can nearly double memory in the worst case.
4. **Only one child at a time.** Redis will not start a second `BGSAVE` or AOF rewrite while one is running; a request is deferred or refused.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Fork cost and Transparent Huge Pages `fork()` copies the process page tables, so the pause grows with dataset size (tens of milliseconds for a few GB on bare metal, more on some virtual machines). On Linux, Transparent Huge Pages (THP) make COW much worse because a one-byte write copies a 2 MB page: latency spikes and memory blow-up during saves. Redis logs a warning at startup if THP is enabled; disable it as the warning advises. Also set `vm.overcommit_memory = 1`, otherwise `fork()` can fail on a busy machine even though the child would barely use memory.

### Observing and tuning

`INFO persistence` is the place to look. The fields that matter:

rows: Writes since the last successful snapshot: your current "at risk" count
Unix time of the last successful save (also available as LASTSAVE)
ok or err; alert if not ok
How long the last save took
Duration of the last fork in microseconds: the main-thread pause

blocks.text:
`stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes` deserves attention. If the disk is full or read-only, the next write is refused with `MISCONF Redis is configured to save RDB snapshots, but it's currently unable to persist to disk`. That error is Redis protecting you from silently running without a backup. Fix the disk problem; turning the setting off just hides it.

### What is inside the file

You do not need to parse RDB files by hand, but knowing the layout explains why loading is fast. The file starts with the magic string `REDIS` followed by a four-digit format version (for example `REDIS0010` on 7.0). Then come auxiliary fields (Redis version, creation time, memory used), and for each database a selector followed by the key-value pairs. Each pair is stored as an optional expiry (absolute time), a one-byte type, the key, and the value in a serialised form that reuses the compact encodings (a listpack is dumped almost as it is in memory). The file ends with an end marker and the CRC64 checksum.

Because the format is dense and mostly a straight copy, loading an RDB is typically much faster than replaying a log of commands. The same format is used for replica synchronization and for the `DUMP`/`RESTORE` commands of a single key. Tools: `redis-check-rdb` verifies a file, and `redis-cli --rdb out.rdb` downloads a snapshot from a running server over the network.

Restoring is simple: stop Redis, put the file at `dir/dbfilename`, start Redis. If AOF is enabled, Redis loads the AOF instead (see the next chapter), so remember to account for that.

### A restore drill

The only way to know a backup works is to restore it. This short drill uses a snapshot from a test server and checks it with the bundled tool before loading.

blocks.code:

blocks.text:
Then restore:

1. Stop the target server (`redis-cli SHUTDOWN NOSAVE`, so it does not overwrite the file you are about to copy with its own empty dataset).
2. Copy the backup to `dir/dbfilename` and check ownership so the `redis` user can read it.
3. Start the server with `appendonly no` for this first load (see the AOF chapters for why).
4. Verify: `DBSIZE`, a handful of known keys, and `INFO persistence` showing `loading:0`.

Large files take time to load, and while loading, Redis answers commands with `-LOADING Redis is loading the` `dataset in memory`. A readiness probe should wait for that to clear.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: A common production use of RDB only Teams that use Redis as a cache of a database, where the data can be rebuilt, often keep RDB with a lazy rule (or `save ""` on replicas) simply so that a restart warms the cache from the last snapshot rather than starting cold. A cold cache can send a stampede of reads to the database.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How can Redis snapshot a multi-GB dataset without blocking clients? It calls `fork()`. The child process gets a copy-on-write view of memory frozen at fork time and writes the RDB file while the parent keeps serving commands. Pages the parent modifies are copied by the kernel so the child's view stays consistent. The only main-thread pause is the fork call itself (page-table copy), and the cost is extra memory proportional to the writes during the save. The file is written to a temp name and atomically renamed.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- An RDB file is a compact point-in-time snapshot; loading is fast, but data after the last snapshot is lost in a crash.
- `BGSAVE` forks a child and uses copy-on-write; `SAVE` blocks the server and is for maintenance only.
- Snapshots are triggered by `save <seconds> <changes>` rules, by `SHUTDOWN` and by replica full syncs.
- Watch `rdb_last_bgsave_status`, `rdb_changes_since_last_save` and `latest_fork_usec`; disable THP and set `vm.overcommit_memory = 1`.
- Keep `dir` on a persistent volume; copy snapshots off the machine for backups.

Snapshots lose minutes of writes. For data like order events or carts that is often unacceptable. The **append-only file** (AOF) takes the opposite approach: instead of photographing the dataset, it keeps a *journal* of every write command, in order. To recover, Redis replays the journal from start to end. The loss window shrinks from minutes to about a second, or to zero at the highest cost.

### How the AOF works

Every command that modifies data is, after it executes, serialised in the same RESP format clients use and appended to an in-memory AOF buffer. Before the loop sleeps, Redis writes the buffer to the file with `write()`, which hands the bytes to the operating system's page cache. A second step, `fsync()`, forces the OS to push them to the physical disk. *When* Redis calls `fsync` is the `appendfsync` policy, and it is the single most important durability setting you will touch.

blocks.caption: appendfsync policies.

blocks.text:
Important subtleties:

- A process crash (Redis killed with `kill -9`) loses *less* than a power failure or kernel crash, because bytes already passed to `write()` are in the OS cache and survive the death of the Redis process. `fsync` protects against the machine going down.
- With `everysec`, if the background `fsync` takes longer than a second, Redis may delay writes to the file rather than let the backlog grow unbounded. In that pathological case the loss window can be about two seconds. `INFO` `persistence` exposes `aof_delayed_fsync`, a counter of such events.
- Disk latency is not Redis latency, but it can become it: a slow shared disk plus `always` makes every write wait.

You turn the AOF on in `redis.conf`; it is **off by default**:

blocks.code:
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec
appenddirname appendonlydir      # directory (inside dir) for the AOF files
aof-use-rdb-preamble yes         # base file is an RDB snapshot (compact, fast to load)
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100  # rewrite when file grew by 100% since last rewrite
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb   # ...and is at least this big
blocks.title: redis.conf

blocks.text:
You can also start it on a running server with `CONFIG SET appendonly yes`, which triggers a rewrite to create the first base file. Edit `redis.conf` as well (or use `CONFIG REWRITE`) so the setting survives a restart.

### Multi-part AOF (Redis 7.0 and later)

Before 7.0 the AOF was one file and rewriting it needed an in-memory "rewrite buffer" plus careful double writing. Since 7.0 the AOF is a **directory** of files tracked by a manifest:

- one **base** file (at most one): a snapshot of the dataset at the time of the last rewrite, in RDB format when `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes` (the default) or as plain commands otherwise;
- one or more **incremental** files: the commands written since that base;
- a **manifest** that lists them in order.

Here is a real directory after a rewrite and one more write, on a test server:

blocks.code:
$ ls appendonlydir
appendonly.aof.2.base.rdb  appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof  appendonly.aof.manifest
$ cat appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.manifest
file appendonly.aof.2.base.rdb seq 2 type b
file appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof seq 2 type i
$ head -8 appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof
*2
$6
SELECT
$1
0
*2
$4
incr
blocks.title: The AOF directory and its manifest

blocks.text:
The incremental file shows the RESP format: `*2` means an array of two items, `$4` a 4-byte string. It is readable, and it is why people can repair it by hand when needed. A `SELECT 0` line appears because the AOF records which database the following commands apply to.

At startup Redis reads the manifest, loads the base (an RDB load, fast), then replays the incremental files in order.

### Rewrite: keeping the file small

The log only grows. `INCR counter` a million times creates a million lines, though the state is one number. **Rewriting** produces a new, minimal base from the current dataset and starts a fresh incremental file.

blocks.text:
Step by step in 7.0 and later:

1. Redis opens a **new incremental file** so that new writes go there from now on, and forks a child (`BGREWRITEAOF`, or automatic).
2. The child writes a **new base file** with the dataset as of the fork. With the RDB preamble this is a standard RDB dump.
3. When the child finishes, the parent updates the manifest atomically: new base plus the new incremental file(s), and marks the old files for deletion.

Automatic rewrites trigger when the AOF has grown by `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage` (100 means it doubled) since the last rewrite and is at least `auto-aof-rewrite-min-size` (64 MB). The cost of a rewrite is the same as `BGSAVE`: a fork, copy-on-write memory, and disk I/O. `aof_rewrite_in_progress` and `aof_last_bgrewrite_status` in `INFO persistence` tell you the state; the rewrite will not start while a `BGSAVE` is running (the request is deferred).

Directives that influence the disk behaviour:
