blocks.caption: AOF tuning.

blocks.text:
### Experiment: kill -9 and recover

Seeing the AOF work is more convincing than reading about it. Start a server with the AOF on, decrement a flash-sale stock counter three times, wait a moment, kill the process without any chance to clean up, and start it again from the same directory.

blocks.code:
$ redis-server --appendonly yes --appendfsync everysec --dir /tmp/aofdemo --daemonize yes
$ redis-cli SET stock:sku42 100
OK
$ redis-cli DECR stock:sku42
(integer) 99
$ redis-cli DECR stock:sku42
(integer) 98
$ redis-cli DECR stock:sku42
(integer) 97
$ sleep 2; pkill -9 redis-server
$ redis-server --appendonly yes --dir /tmp/aofdemo --daemonize yes
$ redis-cli GET stock:sku42
"97"
blocks.title: A crash does not lose acknowledged, fsynced writes

blocks.text:
With RDB only and default save rules (nothing triggered by four writes), the same experiment returns `(nil)`, because no snapshot had been taken. If you skip the `sleep 2` the result is still very likely 97, since a killed process leaves bytes already handed to the kernel; to really lose the last second you must cut power to the machine. That distinction between a process crash and a machine crash is the most common source of confusion about `everysec`.

### What fsync guarantees (and does not)

`fsync` asks the operating system to flush a file's data to the storage device and wait. Three caveats keep your expectations realistic.

- Some disks and virtual disks acknowledge a flush while the data still sits in a volatile write cache. The guarantee is only as good as the storage stack; cloud block storage and battery-backed controllers are usually fine, cheap consumer drives may not be.
- `fsync` of the AOF does not make a *replica* consistent. Writes acknowledged by the primary's disk may never have reached any replica when the primary dies.
- Durability and consistency are separate: the AOF can only replay what was logged. A command that failed halfway through (for instance a `MULTI` block that contains an error that appears at runtime) is logged as it executed, which is how Redis transactions behave (see the transactions chapter).

### Corruption and repair

The most common problem is a **truncated tail**: the machine lost power while a command was half written. With `aof-load-truncated yes` Redis starts anyway, discards the incomplete last command, and logs what it did:

blocks.code:
# !!! Warning: short read while loading the AOF file appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof!!!
# !!! Truncating the AOF appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof at offset 44 !!!
# AOF appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof loaded anyway because aof-load-truncated is enabled
blocks.title: Redis log when it loads a torn AOF (aof-load-truncated yes)

blocks.text: Corruption in the middle of the file is different: Redis refuses to start, because loading the rest would produce a dataset with a hole. Use the checker, first without changing anything:

blocks.code:
$ redis-check-aof appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.manifest
Start checking Multi Part AOF
Start to check BASE AOF (RDB format).
RDB preamble is OK, proceeding with AOF tail...
BASE AOF appendonly.aof.2.base.rdb is valid
Start to check INCR files.
0x              44: Expected to read 7 bytes, got 3 bytes
AOF analyzed: filename=appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof, size=71, ok_up_to=44, ok_up_to_line=17, diff=27
AOF appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof is not valid. Use the --fix option to try fixing it.
$ redis-check-aof --fix appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.manifest
...
This will shrink the AOF appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof from 71 bytes, with 27 bytes, to 44 bytes
Continue? [y/N]: y
Successfully truncated AOF appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof
blocks.title: Check and fix a damaged AOF

blocks.text: (Output condensed; the lines are from a real run on 7.0 except the final confirmation.) The tool reports the offset of the first bad byte (`ok_up_to`) and `--fix` truncates the file there. Read the `diff` number: if it is 27 bytes at the end, you lose one partial command; if it says megabytes, the damage is in the middle and `--fix` discards everything after it. Copy the directory first, always. Related directive: `aof-load-truncated no` makes Redis refuse to start on any truncated tail, if you prefer a human to decide.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Check the disk before trusting `everysec` A full disk makes AOF writes fail. Redis reacts by rejecting writes (`aof_last_write_status:err`) rather than continuing with an incomplete journal. Alert on `aof_last_write_status` and on free disk space, and keep room for a rewrite, which temporarily needs space for the old and new files.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is an AOF rewrite and why is it needed? The AOF is an append-only journal that grows with every write, including overwrites and deletes of the same keys. A rewrite builds a compact new base from the current in-memory state in a forked child (as an RDB preamble), while new writes go to a fresh incremental file, then swaps the manifest. This shrinks the file, speeds up restart, and happens in the background. Since 7.0 the AOF is a base file, incremental files and a manifest.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The AOF logs every write command; `appendfsync` decides the loss window: `always` ≈ none, `everysec` ≈ 1 second, `no` ≈ OS-defined.
- It is off by default (`appendonly no`); enable it for data you cannot lose.
- Since 7.0 it is a directory: base file, incremental files and `appendonly.aof.manifest`.
- Rewrites (`BGREWRITEAOF` or `auto-aof-rewrite-*`) shrink it using a fork, like `BGSAVE`.
- A torn last command is handled by `aof-load-truncated`; use `redis-check-aof` (copy first, then `--fix`) for real corruption.

sections.title: Choosing a Persistence and Durability Strategy

blocks.text:
Persistence settings are a business decision disguised as configuration. Each option moves a point on three scales: how much data you can lose, how fast you recover, and how much performance and operational care you pay. This chapter turns the mechanisms into a decision.

### The four configurations

rows: Pure cache; restart is instant but cold; fastest and simplest
Good for rebuildable data; small files, easy backups
The usual choice when Redis holds data of value
Expect much lower write throughput; test on your disk
AOF is used on restart; RDB is a convenient backup format
blocks.caption: Persistence strategies compared.

blocks.text:
Remember how the restart choice works: if the AOF is enabled and exists, Redis loads **the AOF**, not the RDB, since the AOF is normally more complete. Having both is recommended by the project when you want strong durability, because periodic RDB files give you simple, separate point-in-time backups, while the AOF provides the small loss window.

### Matching strategy to data: ShopStream

You do not have to choose one strategy for the whole system. ShopStream applies different rules to different roles, which in practice means separate Redis deployments (or at least separate instances for separate durability needs):

rows: None, or RDB on a replica
Rebuilt from the database; a cold start costs load, not data
Short-lived and low value; resetting is harmless
Losing a second of cart edits is acceptable; losing everything is not
AOF everysec, RDB backups, replica, possibly WAIT
These events feed notifications and downstream services
AOF everysec or accept loss with TTL logic
Locks expire anyway; lost idempotency keys risk duplicates, so persist them
Source of truth for money or inventory
Keep the system of record in the database; Redis is the fast path
blocks.caption: ShopStream persistence plan.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Persistence is not replication, and neither is a backup Persistence protects against *process or machine restart on the* *same disk*. Replication protects against *losing the node*, but replicates mistakes (a bad `FLUSHALL`) instantly. Backups protect against mistakes and disasters. A serious deployment uses all three. Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost on failover even with `appendfsync always` on the old primary; the replication chapters cover this and `WAIT`.

### Diskless replication and persistence-free replicas

When a replica needs a full sync the primary produces an RDB. By default (`repl-diskless-sync yes`) it streams the RDB directly to the replica sockets from the child process instead of writing a file first, which avoids disk I/O on the primary. A common design is to run the primary with persistence and let the replica persist too, or the reverse: persistence only on replicas so the primary never forks for backups. The risk of the second design is a primary restarting empty and replicating emptiness back to its replicas, so it needs failover automation that prevents the restarted primary from coming back as primary. For beginners, the safe default is to persist on the primary.

### Backups and restores

A backup you have never restored is a hope. Rules that work:

1. **Take consistent files.** An RDB file is a complete snapshot, so copy it with `cp` or `rsync` after a `BGSAVE` finishes (check `rdb_bgsave_in_progress:0`). A running `BGSAVE` replaces the file atomically, so a copy of `dump.rdb` is always complete. For the AOF directory, copy all files together while no rewrite is running (`aof_rewrite_in_progress:0`); the Redis docs suggest temporarily disabling automatic rewrites with `CONFIG SET auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0` during the copy, then restoring the value.
2. **Keep several generations**: hourly for a day, daily for a month, for example, as the persistence documentation proposes with hourly and daily directories.
3. **Move copies off the machine** (another host, another region, object storage), at least once a day.
4. **Verify**: compare size and checksum after transfer, run `redis-check-rdb` or `redis-check-aof`, and on a schedule restore into a scratch instance and read some keys.
5. **Remote snapshot**: `redis-cli --rdb backup.rdb` fetches an RDB from a running server over the network without touching its disk layout.
6. **Document the restore**: stop Redis, remove the old data files, place the backup in `dir`, start, check `DBSIZE` and a few known keys. If the backup is an RDB but AOF is enabled in config, start with `appendonly no`, then enable the AOF through `CONFIG SET appendonly yes` after loading; otherwise Redis will find no AOF and start empty.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: The restore that comes back empty You copy a good `dump.rdb` into the data directory of a server with `appendonly yes`, start Redis, and `DBSIZE` says 0. The server created an empty AOF at first start (or already had one) and loads it in preference to the RDB. Restore the RDB with AOF disabled, verify the data, then turn on the AOF so it generates a base from the loaded dataset.

### Putting numbers on it

A useful exercise is to write the recovery requirements as two numbers: **RPO** (recovery point objective, how much data you may lose, in time) and **RTO** (recovery time objective, how long you may be down). Then map them:

- RPO of a day, RTO of minutes: RDB only, cache semantics, cold-start protection in the application.
- RPO of seconds: AOF `everysec` plus a replica for failover.
- RPO of zero for acknowledged writes: Redis is probably not the right place for that data unless you accept the performance cost of `appendfsync always`, plus synchronous replication via `WAIT`, which narrows but does not eliminate the window. Keep the system of record in a database designed for it.
- Restart time (RTO) scales with dataset size: loading roughly takes seconds per few GB for an RDB base, and longer if there is a large incremental tail, so rewrite regularly. Measure on your hardware with a restore drill.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: The cache that was also the primary store A frequent incident pattern: a team starts with Redis as a cache, gradually stores sessions, then job queues in the same instance, with no persistence and an `allkeys-lru` policy. A restart or an eviction round then loses user sessions and pending jobs. The fix is organisational, not clever: classify data by loss tolerance, give each class its own instance and policy, and write the persistence strategy next to the key schema.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How would you configure Redis so you lose at most about a second of data, and what can still go wrong? Enable the AOF with `appendfsync everysec` (optionally with RDB for backups). A crash then loses roughly one second of writes. Things that can still go wrong: the disk stalls so the delay approaches two seconds; replication is asynchronous so a failover can lose recent writes that never reached the replica (mitigate with `min-replicas-to-write` and `WAIT`); a bug or operator mistake (`FLUSHALL`) is persisted too, so you also need point-in-time backups; and a full disk stops writes. For zero loss, use `appendfsync always` and accept the throughput cost, or keep the data in a database whose guarantees match.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Choose by loss tolerance and recovery time: none (cache), RDB only (minutes), AOF everysec (about 1 second), AOF always (near zero, slow).
- Restart loads the AOF when it is enabled; to restore an RDB into an AOF-enabled server, load with AOF off first.
- Persistence, replication and backups solve different problems; production needs all three.
- Backups must be complete, off-machine, versioned and test-restored; check them with `redis-check-rdb` and `redis-check-aof`.
- Give different data classes (cache, sessions, order stream) different instances and policies.

Sooner or later an application needs to change two or more keys as one unit. A customer checks out: the cart must be emptied and the order counter must go up. A seat is reserved: the seat key is set and the seat count is decremented. If another client can see the state half-way through, or if one of the commands is lost while the others succeed, the data is wrong. Relational databases solve this with transactions. Redis has transactions too, but they are much simpler than the SQL kind, and the differences are exactly what interviewers and production incidents are made of. This chapter explains what a Redis transaction guarantees, what it does not, and how `WATCH` adds optimistic locking on top.

### The core idea: a queued batch executed without interruption

A Redis transaction is a **queue of commands that the server runs back to back, with no other client's** **command in between**. You open the queue with `MULTI`, send the commands (the server answers `QUEUED` to each instead of running it), and run the whole queue with `EXEC`. Because Redis executes commands on a single main thread (see the chapter on the server architecture), nothing else can interleave while `EXEC` is running its queue. That property is called **isolation**, and Redis gets it for free.

blocks.title: A simple transaction

blocks.text: `EXEC` returns an array with one reply per queued command, in order. `DISCARD` throws the queue away and leaves the connection in normal mode. If the connection drops before `EXEC`, the queue is simply forgotten.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: A Redis transaction is a sequence of commands queued with `MULTI` and executed atomically in order by `EXEC`: no other client command runs in between. There is no rollback. Commands that fail at execution time do not undo the commands before them.

### Two kinds of errors, two behaviours

This is the most important part of the chapter. A command in a transaction can fail at two different moments, and Redis treats them differently.

**Errors while queueing.** If a command is syntactically wrong (unknown command, wrong number of arguments), the server refuses it right away with an error. When you later call `EXEC`, Redis refuses to run anything and discards the whole transaction.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> MULTI
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET order:9:status "PAID"
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:6379> FOOBAR
(error) ERR unknown command 'FOOBAR', with args beginning with:
127.0.0.1:6379> EXEC
(error) EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of previous errors.
127.0.0.1:6379> GET order:9:status
(nil)
blocks.title: Error at queue time: nothing runs

blocks.text: **Errors at execution time.** If the command is well formed but fails when it runs, for example `LPUSH` on a key holding a string, then that one command returns an error and **all the others still run**. Redis does not roll back.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET a 1
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> MULTI
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR a
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH a x
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:6379> GET a
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:6379> EXEC
1) (integer) 2
2) (error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value
3) "2"
blocks.title: Error at execution time: the rest still runs

blocks.text: Why no rollback? The Redis authors argue that execution-time errors are programming errors (wrong type, bad argument) that should be caught in development, not at runtime in production, and that skipping rollback keeps Redis simple and fast. You may or may not agree, but you must design for it: a Redis transaction gives you **isolation and** **ordered execution**, not the "all or nothing" part of ACID.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: "Atomic" in Redis means "no other client's command interleaves", not "all commands succeed or none do". If command 2 of 3 fails at execution time, commands 1 and 3 have already taken effect and stay. Do not rely on `MULTI` to undo partial work. If you need a conditional, all-or-nothing update that depends on the data, use a Lua script or a function (next chapters).

There is one more case worth knowing. If the server crashes or is killed in the middle of `EXEC`, the persistence layer may hold only part of the transaction. With AOF, a half-written transaction is detected at restart and the server refuses to load until you repair the file with `redis-check-aof`. This is rare, but it is the reason the word "atomic" needs the footnote above.

### No reads inside the decision: the problem WATCH solves

A transaction queues commands; it does not give you their results until `EXEC`. That means you cannot read a value, decide something in your application, and write it back inside the same transaction. Consider decrementing a stock counter only if it is positive:

blocks.code:
GET stock:sku-77        → 1          (client A reads)
GET stock:sku-77        → 1          (client B reads)
DECR stock:sku-77       → 0          (A buys the last unit)
DECR stock:sku-77       → -1         (B buys it too: oversold)

blocks.text:
The read and the write are separate steps and another client can slip in between. `MULTI` alone cannot help, because the `GET` result is not available until after `EXEC`. This is a classic **check-then-act race condition**.

`WATCH` solves it with **optimistic locking**. You tell Redis which keys you care about, then read them normally, decide, and then run a transaction. If any watched key was modified by anyone (including expiry or eviction) between your `WATCH` and your `EXEC`, the `EXEC` does nothing and returns a null reply. You then retry the whole read-decide-write cycle.
If a second client had run `DECR stock:sku-77` after the `WATCH`, our `EXEC` would have printed `(nil)` and executed nothing. The code that uses this is always a loop:

blocks.code:
loop (max N times):
    WATCH key
    value = GET key              # plain read, outside MULTI
    if value is not good enough: UNWATCH; give up
    MULTI
    write commands based on value
    result = EXEC
    if result is not null: done
    # otherwise somebody changed the key: try again

blocks.text:
It is called optimistic because it does not block anyone: it assumes conflicts are rare and pays only when one happens. Under high contention on one key (a flash sale for a single SKU), many attempts fail and retry, which wastes round trips. In that situation a single Lua script (the next chapter) is far better.

#### Rules of WATCH

- `WATCH` must be sent before `MULTI`. Calling it inside `MULTI` is an error.
- `EXEC` and `DISCARD` forget all watched keys, and so does `UNWATCH`. `WATCH` is per connection, so it needs a connection that is not shared between threads at that moment.
- A watched key counts as modified when it is written, deleted, expires, or is evicted. Since Redis 6.0.9, a key that was already expired when `WATCH` ran does not trigger a false abort later. A write that does not change the value (for example `SET` with the same value) still counts as a touch.
- Watching a key in one logical database and switching with `SELECT` is not a safe pattern; use one database.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: In Redis Cluster all keys of a transaction (and all watched keys) must live in the same hash slot, or you get a `CROSSSLOT` error. Use hash tags such as `cart:{1001}:items` and `cart:{1001}:meta` so related keys land in the same slot. The chapter on Redis Cluster in the scaling part explains slots in detail.

### Transactions versus pipelines

Both `MULTI/EXEC` and pipelining send several commands in one network trip, so people confuse them. They solve different problems:

rows: Yes: send MULTI ... EXEC inside a pipeline
blocks.caption: Transaction versus pipeline.

blocks.text: Most client libraries pipeline the whole `MULTI` ... `EXEC` block automatically, so you pay one round trip. You will see how in the Java client chapters and in the Spring chapter on transactions and scripts.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Does Redis support transactions? Are they ACID? Redis supports transactions through `MULTI`, `EXEC`, `DISCARD` and `WATCH`. Commands in a transaction run sequentially and in isolation, because the command loop is single threaded, so no other client interleaves. But there is no rollback: a command that fails at execution time does not undo the others, so it is not atomic in the "all or nothing" sense. `WATCH` adds optimistic check-and-set. Durability depends on the persistence settings. For conditional logic that must be atomic, use a Lua script or a function.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `MULTI` queues commands and `EXEC` runs them back to back; nothing from other clients runs in between.
- Syntax errors found while queueing abort the whole transaction; runtime errors (such as `WRONGTYPE`) do not roll anything back.
- You cannot make decisions on read results inside `MULTI`; use `WATCH` for optimistic check-and-set and retry on a null `EXEC` reply.
- Under contention on a single key, prefer a Lua script or function to a `WATCH` retry loop.
- Transactions are not pipelines: one gives isolation, the other saves round trips. In Cluster, keep all keys in one slot.

Transactions cannot branch on data. Pipelines cannot either. Many real operations need exactly that: "decrement the stock only if there is enough, and tell me what happened", "release the lock only if I still own it", "refill a token bucket based on elapsed time". Doing these from the client means several round trips and a race condition between them. **Lua scripting** lets you ship a small program to the server and run it there, as one indivisible step. It is the main tool for building correct compound operations in Redis, and it appears throughout the patterns and projects parts of this book.

### What a script is and how it runs

Redis embeds the Lua 5.1 interpreter. `EVAL` sends the script text, the number of key arguments, the key names, then extra arguments:

blocks.code: EVAL script numkeys [key [key ...]] [arg [arg ...]]

127.0.0.1:6379> SET stock:sku-77 10
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> EVAL "return redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])" 1 stock:sku-77
"10"
127.0.0.1:6379> EVAL "return ARGV[1] .. '-' .. ARGV[2]" 0 hello world
"hello-world"
blocks.title: Your first script

blocks.text:
Inside the script, the global tables `KEYS` and `ARGV` hold the key names and the other arguments (Lua arrays start at 1, and every element is a string). The function `redis.call(command, ...)` runs any Redis command and returns its reply converted to a Lua value.

The crucial property: **while a script runs, the server executes nothing else.** It behaves like a transaction that can contain `if` statements and loops. Everything the script reads is guaranteed not to change under its feet, and its writes become visible together.

### KEYS versus ARGV

Pass every key the script touches in `KEYS`, and everything else (amounts, tokens, timestamps, TTLs) in `ARGV`. This is not decoration:

- Redis Cluster uses the declared keys to route the call to the right shard and to check that all keys live in one slot.
- Tools, ACLs and replicas use the declared keys to understand what the script accesses.
- It keeps scripts reusable: the same script text works for any key name.

Scripts that build key names dynamically inside the code (for example `redis.call('GET', 'user:' .. ARGV[1])`) may appear to work on a single node and then fail in Cluster. Declare keys properly from day one.

### redis.call versus redis.pcall, and return values

If a command run with `redis.call` fails, the error is raised and the script aborts with that error. `redis.pcall` ("protected call") catches the error and returns it as a table with an `err` field, so the script can handle it.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET sku "x"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> EVAL "return redis.call('LPUSH', KEYS[1], 'a')" 1 sku
(error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value script: ...
127.0.0.1:6379> EVAL "return redis.pcall('LPUSH', KEYS[1], 'a')" 1 sku
(error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value
blocks.title: call aborts, pcall returns the error

blocks.text:
Writes made before an error are **not rolled back**, just as in `MULTI`. Order your script so that checks come first and writes last.

Return values are converted between Lua and the Redis protocol. The table to remember:

rows: `array reply; stops at the first nil`
blocks.caption: How Lua values become Redis replies.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Returning a Lua number truncates it to an integer, and `false` becomes a nil reply, not 0. If you need a decimal, return it as a string with `tostring(x)`. If you want to return "false" to the client, return the integer 0 instead. Converting the other way, a Redis integer reply becomes a Lua number, a bulk string becomes a Lua string and a nil bulk reply becomes Lua `false`, so test with `if not value then`.

### Script cache: EVALSHA and SCRIPT LOAD

Sending the script text on every call wastes bandwidth. When Redis runs a script, it caches it under its **SHA1 hash**. `SCRIPT LOAD` caches without running and returns the hash; `EVALSHA` runs by hash:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SCRIPT LOAD "return redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])"
"d3c21d0c2b9ca22f82737626a27bcaf5d288f99f"
127.0.0.1:6379> EVALSHA d3c21d0c2b9ca22f82737626a27bcaf5d288f99f 1 stock:sku-77
"10"
127.0.0.1:6379> EVALSHA ffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff 0
(error) NOSCRIPT No matching script. Please use EVAL.
blocks.title: Load once, call by hash

blocks.text:
The cache lives only in memory. It is **not** persisted by RDB, and a restart, a failover to a replica that never ran the script, or `SCRIPT FLUSH` empties it. Client libraries therefore follow the pattern: try `EVALSHA`; on `NOSCRIPT`, send `EVAL` (which also repopulates the cache). Spring's `DefaultRedisScript` and Redisson do this for you. Do not generate script text dynamically with values pasted in; each variant would be cached separately and fill memory. Always pass variable data through `KEYS` and `ARGV`.

### Determinism and replication

Older Redis versions replicated scripts by re-running the script text on replicas and in the AOF, so scripts had to be deterministic (same input, same result) and `TIME` or `SRANDMEMBER` before a write was forbidden. Since Redis 5 replication ships by default (and 7.0 removed the old mode) the script's **effects**, that is, the write commands it actually performed. Consequently you can use `redis.call('TIME')` and random commands freely in modern versions. The rule that remains: the script must not depend on the clock of the machine or on global state outside Redis in ways you want replicated, because only the commands it issued are copied.

### Limits you must respect

- **A script blocks the server.** Because nothing else runs, a slow script is an outage. The setting `busy-reply-threshold` (older name `lua-time-limit`, default 5000 ms) is not a limit that kills the script: it is the time after which Redis starts replying `BUSY` to other clients and begins to accept `SCRIPT KILL` (for scripts that have not written yet) or `SHUTDOWN NOSAVE`.
- **Keep scripts short.** A handful of commands and loops bounded by a small known number. Never loop over an unbounded collection.
- **No blocking commands.** `BLPOP` and friends behave as their non-blocking counterparts inside scripts.
- **Cluster key rule.** All keys must hash to one slot, and must be declared in `KEYS`.
- **Global variables are forbidden.** Declare everything with `local`. Redis protects its global table and raises an error on accidental globals.
- **Scripts are not a place for business logic.** They are for small atomic read-modify-write operations. Everything else belongs in the application.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> EVAL "while true do end" 0
# (blocks; from another client, after the threshold)
127.0.0.1:6379> GET stock:sku-77
(error) BUSY Redis is busy running a script. You can only call SCRIPT KILL or SHUTDOWN NOSAVE.
127.0.0.1:6379> SCRIPT KILL
OK
blocks.title: A runaway script and how to stop it
Watch out
blocks.text: If a script has already performed a write, `SCRIPT KILL` is refused (to protect atomicity) and your only escape is `SHUTDOWN` `NOSAVE`, which loses unsaved data. Test every script against realistic data sizes before it goes live.

### Pattern 1: compare-and-delete (safe lock release)

A distributed lock is stored as `lock:order:5001` with a random token as its value. To release it, you must delete the key only if it still holds your token; otherwise you might delete a lock that expired and was acquired by someone else. `GET` followed by `DEL` from the client is racy, so do it in Lua. This is the textbook script:

blocks.code:
-- KEYS[1] = lock key, ARGV[1] = owner token
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end
blocks.title: release_lock.lua

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET lock:order:5001 "token-abc" NX PX 30000
OK
$ redis-cli --eval release_lock.lua lock:order:5001 , token-xyz
(integer) 0
$ redis-cli --eval release_lock.lua lock:order:5001 , token-abc
(integer) 1
blocks.title: Run it
Note
blocks.text: Redis 8.4 added `DELEX` and the `IFEQ` option of `SET`, which implement compare-and-delete and compare-and-set natively. With them the script above can become a single `DELEX lock:order:5001 IFEQ token-abc`. Check the command pages for your exact version before depending on them, and keep the Lua version if you must support older servers. The chapter on distributed locks in the Patterns part builds on this.

### Pattern 2: atomic stock decrement for a flash sale

The ShopStream flash sale must never oversell. The script checks the stock and decrements it in one step, returning the new stock or -1 when there is not enough:

blocks.code:
-- KEYS[1] = stock counter (stock:{sku}), ARGV[1] = quantity wanted
local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]))
local want = tonumber(ARGV[1])
if stock == nil then
  return -2              -- key missing: unknown SKU
end
if stock < want then
  return -1              -- not enough stock, nothing changed
end
return redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], want)
blocks.title: reserve_stock.lua

blocks.text:
What to notice: the read, the comparison and the write are one atomic step, so two buyers can never both take the last unit. The distinct return codes (-2, -1, remaining count) let the caller tell "unknown product" from "sold out" without a second round trip. The full flash-sale project later in the book extends this with reservations and a TTL.

### Pattern 3: token bucket rate limiter

A token bucket allows bursts up to a capacity and refills at a steady rate. State (current tokens and last refill time) lives in one hash. The script computes the refill from the time elapsed, so no background process is needed:

blocks.code:
-- KEYS[1] = bucket hash, e.g. rl:{ip}:{route}
-- ARGV[1] = capacity, ARGV[2] = refill tokens per second, ARGV[3] = tokens requested
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)   -- milliseconds

local data = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1])
local ts = tonumber(data[2])
if tokens == nil then
  tokens = capacity
  ts = now
end

local elapsed = math.max(0, now - ts)
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * rate / 1000)

local allowed = 0
if tokens >= requested then
  tokens = tokens - requested
  allowed = 1
end

redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tostring(tokens), 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / rate * 1000) * 2)
return {allowed, math.floor(tokens)}
blocks.title: token_bucket.lua

blocks.text:
What to notice: `TIME` is read inside the script, so all application servers share one clock (the Redis server's) and clock skew between them does not matter. The `PEXPIRE` makes idle buckets disappear. The token count is stored with `tostring` so that the fractional part is kept as text. The rate limiting chapter in the Patterns part compares this with fixed and sliding windows.

### Calling scripts and debugging

From the shell, keep the script in a file and let `redis-cli` read it. Note the comma that separates keys from arguments in this mode:

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli --eval token_bucket.lua rl:10.0.0.7:checkout , 20 5 1
1) (integer) 1
2) (integer) 19
blocks.title: Run a script file with redis-cli

blocks.text: For stepping through a script, `redis-cli --ldb --eval file.lua keys , args` starts the Redis Lua debugger; use it on a development instance only. Inside scripts, `redis.log(redis.LOG_WARNING, "message")` writes to the server log, and `redis.sha1hex(str)` is available. Calling `redis.setresp(3)` switches the reply format that `redis.call` returns, which matters only for RESP3 maps and sets.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why use a Lua script instead of MULTI/EXEC with WATCH? A script runs the whole read-decide-write sequence atomically on the server in a single round trip and never retries. `WATCH` needs at least two round trips and retries under contention, and each retry repeats the read. Scripts pay with server time: a long script blocks every other client, so keep them tiny and bounded.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A script runs atomically: no other command executes while it runs, so it can read, decide and write safely.
- Declare every key in `KEYS`, pass everything else in `ARGV`; this is required for Cluster correctness.
- `redis.call` raises errors, `redis.pcall` returns them; there is no rollback of earlier writes.
- Call scripts with `EVALSHA` and fall back to `EVAL` on `NOSCRIPT`; the script cache is lost on restart.
- Keep scripts short and bounded, because a slow script blocks the whole server (`BUSY`).
- Classic uses: compare-and-delete lock release, atomic stock decrement, token bucket.

`EVAL` has an operational weakness: the scripts live in your application code, and each application instance has to send them (or load them into the script cache) by itself. Redis 7.0 introduced **Functions** to treat server-side code as part of the database. A function is stored in the server as a named, versioned-by-you piece of code, persisted and replicated with the data, and called by name. Same Lua engine, same atomic execution, different packaging.

### Libraries and registered functions

Functions are grouped in **libraries**. You write a library as a Lua source with a special first line (the shebang) that names the engine and the library, and inside it you register one or more functions:

blocks.code:
#!lua name=shop

local function reserve_stock(keys, args)
  local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', keys[1]))
  local want = tonumber(args[1])
  if stock == nil then
    return -2
  end
  if stock < want then
    return -1
  end
  return redis.call('DECRBY', keys[1], want)
end

local function stock_level(keys, args)
  return redis.call('GET', keys[1])
end

redis.register_function('reserve_stock', reserve_stock)
redis.register_function{
  function_name = 'stock_level',
  callback = stock_level,
  flags = { 'no-writes' }
}
blocks.title: shop.lua

blocks.text:
What to notice: a function receives two Lua tables, `keys` and `args`, instead of the globals `KEYS` and `ARGV`. A library must register at least one function, or loading fails. The second registration uses the table form so it can attach **flags**; `no-writes` declares that the function never writes, which allows calling it with `FCALL_RO` and on read-only replicas.

### Loading and calling

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli -x FUNCTION LOAD REPLACE < shop.lua
"shop"
127.0.0.1:6379> SET stock:sku-77 10
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL reserve_stock 1 stock:sku-77 3
(integer) 7
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL reserve_stock 1 stock:sku-77 30
(integer) -1
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL_RO stock_level 1 stock:sku-77
"7"
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL_RO reserve_stock 1 stock:sku-77 1
(error) ERR Can not execute a script with write flag using *_ro command.
blocks.title: Load a library and call its functions

blocks.text:
`FCALL function numkeys key... arg...` has the same shape as `EVAL`, but takes a function name instead of source text, so there is no hash to manage and no `NOSCRIPT` fallback. `FUNCTION LOAD` fails if a library with the same name exists unless you pass `REPLACE`.

The management commands you will use:

rows: Load (or replace) a library; returns the library name
Show libraries and their functions and flags
Remove a library and its functions
Serialize all libraries to a payload and load it elsewhere
Show the running function (if any) and engine counts
Stop a running function that has not yet written (like SCRIPT KILL)
blocks.caption: Function management commands.

blocks.text:
### Persistence, replication and clusters

Unlike the EVAL script cache, loaded functions are **persisted in the AOF and in RDB files and replicated to** **replicas**. After a restart or a failover they are still there. That removes the NOSCRIPT dance. Two caveats follow:

- **Cache-only instances.** If the instance has no persistence and restarts empty, the functions are gone. Load them again at deployment time, or extract them into an RDB with `redis-cli --functions-rdb` so the server loads them at startup.
- **Redis Cluster.** Functions are replicated from a primary to its replicas, but loading them on every shard is your job. The deployment pipeline must run `FUNCTION LOAD REPLACE` against every primary node, and be able to handle a node added later.

### EVAL or FUNCTION?

rows: In the server, as named libraries
Sent at runtime, cached by SHA1
Shared local functions inside a library
Script text is its own version
Shared, stable logic used by several services
blocks.caption: EVAL scripts versus Functions.

blocks.text: The trade-off is governance. With `EVAL` the application and its script are released together and cannot drift apart. With Functions the library is a deployment artefact that must exist in every environment before the application that calls it. For a single service, `EVAL` through a library such as Spring's `RedisScript` is perfectly fine. Teams with several services that share atomic operations (stock handling used by cart, order and inventory services) benefit from Functions. Do this carefully: a function replaced in production changes behaviour for every caller at once, so treat `FUNCTION LOAD` `REPLACE` like a database migration, and keep the library source in version control.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Name libraries by domain and bake a version into function names when behaviour changes incompatibly, for example `reserve_stock_v2`. Roll out the new library, switch callers, then delete the old function. That makes rollback a configuration change.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between EVAL and Redis Functions? Both run Lua atomically on the server. `EVAL` scripts are sent by the client and cached by hash in a volatile cache. Functions, added in 7.0, are stored server-side in named libraries, persisted in the AOF and RDB, replicated, and invoked by name with `FCALL`. They suit shared logic managed as part of the database. In Cluster you must load them on every node yourself.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Functions are named Lua code stored in libraries inside Redis, called with `FCALL` and `FCALL_RO`.
- A library starts with a `#!lua name=...` line and registers functions with `redis.register_function`.
- Functions are persisted and replicated, so there is no script-cache loss and no `NOSCRIPT` handling.
- Mark read-only functions with the `no-writes` flag so they can run via `FCALL_RO` and on replicas.
- In Cluster, load libraries on every node; treat library changes as database migrations.

Redis executes most commands in microseconds, yet a real application often sees milliseconds per call. The missing time is not spent inside Redis; it is spent on the network. This chapter shows how to do the arithmetic, how to cut round trips with **pipelining**, what **blocking commands** do (and do not) block, and how to find the cause when Redis really is slow.

### Round-trip time dominates

Every command sent in the usual request-response style costs one **round-trip time (RTT)**: the client writes the command, the packet crosses the network, the server runs it, and the reply crosses back. Within one data centre an RTT is typically a fraction of a millisecond up to about a millisecond; across availability zones or regions it is more. Compare it with the server's own work, which for `GET` or `HSET` is a few microseconds.

Suppose the RTT is 0.5 ms (an illustrative figure) and you need to load 100 product hashes for a category page:

rows: 0.5 ms + server work (a little more for sending and parsing)
blocks.caption: Sequential versus pipelined, illustrative numbers for an RTT of 0.5 ms.

blocks.text:
The server time is the same in all cases; only the waiting changes. A single connection that sends one command at a time can never exceed 1 / RTT commands per second, no matter how fast Redis is. With a 0.5 ms RTT that is a ceiling of about 2,000 commands per second per connection. This is the number-one reason people think "Redis is slow" when it is not, and it is also why an N+1 query pattern against Redis hurts just as much as it does against SQL.

### Pipelining

**Pipelining** means sending many commands without waiting for each reply, then reading all the replies together. The server still executes the commands one after another and queues the replies in an output buffer, but the network is used far more efficiently. It also reduces the number of `read` and `write` system calls on the server, which is why pipelined throughput can be several times higher than non-pipelined throughput even on localhost.

blocks.code:
Without pipelining                      With pipelining
client            server                client            server
  | --- GET a --->  |                     | --- GET a --->  |
  | <-- "1" ------  |                     | --- GET b --->  |
  | --- GET b --->  |                     | --- GET c --->  |
  | <-- "2" ------  |                     | <-- "1" ------  |
  | --- GET c --->  |                     | <-- "2" ------  |
  | <-- "3" ------  |                     | <-- "3" ------  |
  3 round trips                           1 round trip

blocks.text: You can try pipelining with nothing but `redis-cli`. The `--pipe` mode reads commands in the raw Redis protocol, or inline text, from standard input and sends them in bulk. It is the fastest way to load a large file of commands:

blocks.code:
$ for i in $(seq 1 100000); do echo "SET product:$i:stock 50"; done | redis-cli --pipe
All data transferred. Waiting for the last reply...
Last reply received from server.
errors: 0, replies: 100000
blocks.title: Bulk load with redis-cli --pipe

blocks.text: In application code you rarely write protocol by hand. Your client library does it. With Lettuce, the commands you issue on one connection through the async API are pipelined automatically; for explicit batching you turn off auto-flush, issue the commands, and flush once:

blocks.title: PipelineExample.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: the connection is shared, so switching off auto-flush affects every thread using it. That is acceptable in a short-lived, dedicated connection but dangerous on a shared one; the Lettuce chapter in the Java part discusses this trade-off, and Spring's `executePipelined` (see the chapter on transactions and scripts in Spring) hides it behind a safer API.

#### How big should a pipeline be?

Do not pipeline a million commands in one go. The server must hold all the replies in memory before it can send them, and the client must buffer the commands it has not yet sent. A good rule is batches of a few hundred to a few thousand commands: the gain from batching flattens out quickly, while memory use keeps growing linearly. The `redis-cli` `--pipe` tool and `redis-benchmark -P` show the effect; the benchmarking lab in the labs part lets you measure it on your own machine.

#### Pipelines versus transactions, again

A pipeline is not atomic: other clients' commands can be executed between yours. If you need isolation, wrap the batch in `MULTI` and `EXEC` (see the chapter on transactions). If you need a decision inside the batch, use a script. Many libraries combine these (a pipelined transaction), but keep the concepts separate in your head.

### Client output buffers

Every connection has an **output buffer** on the server holding replies that have not yet been delivered. A slow reader, a huge pipeline reply, a `KEYS` result or a subscriber that cannot keep up makes this buffer grow, using server memory. To protect itself, Redis puts limits on it through `client-output-buffer-limit`, one line per client class. The usual defaults are:

blocks.caption: Default client-output-buffer-limit (hard limit, soft limit, soft seconds).

blocks.text:
A client is disconnected when it reaches the hard limit, or stays above the soft limit for the soft period. Normal clients have no limit at all by default, so a client that issues a command with a gigantic reply and reads slowly can consume a lot of memory. Watch the `omem` field of `CLIENT LIST`, the `client_recent_max_output_buffer` value of `INFO clients`, and consider limiting normal clients on shared instances. Also avoid giant replies in the first place: iterate with `SCAN` and its relatives and use `HSCAN`/`SSCAN` instead of `HGETALL`/`SMEMBERS` on large collections.

### Blocking commands

Some commands wait for data to appear: `BLPOP`, `BRPOP`, `BLMOVE`, `BLMPOP`, `BZPOPMIN`, `BZMPOP`, and `XREAD`/`XREADGROUP` with the `BLOCK` option. They exist so that a consumer can wait for work without polling. Their syntax always includes a timeout; `0` means wait forever (in seconds for the list commands, in milliseconds for `BLOCK` on streams).

The key point is what exactly blocks. **Only the calling client waits. The server is not blocked**: it keeps processing other clients' commands while the consumer sleeps. Redis parks the blocked connection in a list per key and wakes it, first come first served, when a producer pushes data.

blocks.code:
# Terminal A (consumer)
127.0.0.1:6379> BLPOP queue:emails 30
# ... waits ...
# Terminal B (producer)
127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH queue:emails "welcome:user-42"
(integer) 1
# Terminal A now prints
1) "queue:emails"
2) "welcome:user-42"
(7.45s)
blocks.title: A blocked consumer, and a producer waking it

blocks.text:
If nothing arrives within the timeout the reply is `(nil)`. Things to know when using blocking commands in an application:

- **A blocked connection is occupied.** It cannot run other commands while it waits. Give each blocking consumer its own dedicated connection and never take it from a general-purpose pool, or you will starve ordinary requests. Lettuce users must not run blocking calls on the shared connection that serves the rest of the application.
- **Set the client read timeout above the block time.** If your client's socket timeout is 5 seconds and you block for 30, the client gives up first. Use a finite block time (5 to 30 seconds) in a loop; it makes shutdown and reconnection logic simple.
- **Blocking commands inside** `MULTI`**, scripts and functions do not block.** They behave like their non-blocking variants and return immediately, otherwise they would freeze the whole server.
- **They are not reliable queues by themselves.** `BLPOP` removes the element before your code processes it; if the worker dies, the job is lost. The patterns part shows `BLMOVE` and streams for reliable processing.

`INFO clients` reports `blocked_clients`, and the `timeout` setting in `redis.conf` closes idle (not blocked) connections; leave it at 0 unless you know why you need it.

### Where latency comes from

When someone says "Redis is slow", first find out which of the following it is. Most cases fall into a handful of causes.

rows: Fast server, slow application; many small calls
Pipeline, use MGET/HMGET, batch work, keep Redis close to the app
Latency spikes, high CPU in the main thread, entries in SLOWLOG
Avoid O(N) commands on big keys; use SCAN family; split big keys
Rare commands take hundreds of ms; output buffers grow
Find with redis-cli --bigkeys; paginate; use UNLINK instead of DEL
Fork for RDB or AOF rewrite
Periodic stalls, worse with large datasets and slow virtualization
Watch latest\_fork\_usec; give memory headroom; schedule snapshots; see persistence chapters
Latency tied to appendfsync always or a busy disk
Use everysec; faster disk; separate disk
Many keys expiring at the same second; latency at memory limit
Add jitter to TTLs; size maxmemory sensibly
Very high, erratic latency; the OS pages Redis memory to disk
Never allow swap on a Redis host; check used\_memory against RAM
Dedicated cores or proper CPU limits; avoid overcommit
Keep scripts tiny; never leave MONITOR running
blocks.caption: Common sources of latency.

blocks.text:
Remember the consequence of the single-threaded command loop: one slow command delays every client queued behind it. A 200 ms `SMEMBERS` on a million-element set is a 200 ms outage for the whole instance, not just for the caller.

### Measuring: SLOWLOG, LATENCY and latency stats

Redis ships with tools for finding these problems. Start with the slow log.

#### SLOWLOG

The slow log records commands whose **execution time** exceeded `slowlog-log-slower-than` microseconds (default 10000, i.e. 10 ms). It keeps the latest `slowlog-max-len` entries (default 128). The time measured is only the time spent running the command; it does not include waiting in the queue, network time or reading the request.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET slowlog-log-slower-than 5000
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG GET 1
1) 1) (integer) 14
   2) (integer) 1791613380
   3) (integer) 18432
   4) 1) "SMEMBERS"
      2) "tags:all"
   5) "10.0.2.15:52134"
   6) "catalog-service"
127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG LEN
(integer) 14
127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG RESET
OK
blocks.title: Reading the slow log

blocks.text:
Each entry has an id, the Unix time, the duration in microseconds (here 18.4 ms), the command with arguments (long arguments are truncated), the client address and the client name set with `CLIENT SETNAME`. Give every service a connection name; it makes the slow log readable. Setting the threshold to 0 logs everything, which is a quick way to see what an application actually sends, but it also costs, so do it briefly. A negative value disables the log.

#### LATENCY monitor and doctor

The latency monitor records events (fork, AOF fsync, expiry cycles, slow commands) that exceeded a threshold. It is off by default; you switch it on by setting a threshold in milliseconds:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET latency-monitor-threshold 100
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> LATENCY LATEST
1) 1) "fork"
   2) (integer) 1791613400
   3) (integer) 235
   4) (integer) 235
127.0.0.1:6379> LATENCY DOCTOR
Dave, I have observed latency spikes in this Redis instance. ...
blocks.title: Turn on the latency monitor

blocks.text:
`LATENCY LATEST` shows, per event type, the time of the latest spike, its duration and the maximum duration seen, in milliseconds. `LATENCY HISTORY fork` gives time series data and `LATENCY GRAPH fork` draws a small ASCII chart. `LATENCY DOCTOR` writes a human-readable analysis with suggestions. The doctor's tone is jokey, but the content is a useful checklist.

#### Per-command latency percentiles

Since Redis 7.0, `latency-tracking` is on by default and the server keeps a histogram per command. `INFO` `latencystats` shows percentiles (by default p50, p99 and p99.9) in microseconds, and `INFO commandstats` shows call counts, total time and microseconds per call. Percentiles tell you far more than averages: a command averaging 20 microseconds can still have a p99.9 of 20 ms because of the occasional big key.

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli --latency
min: 0, max: 1, avg: 0.11 (1372 samples)
$ redis-cli --latency-history -i 5
$ redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 10
Max latency so far: 5 microseconds.
Max latency so far: 28 microseconds.
blocks.title: Latency from the outside with redis-cli

blocks.text: `--latency` measures round trips with `PING` against the server, so it includes the network. `--intrinsic-latency` measures the baseline delay of the machine itself (the scheduler, virtualization) and must be run **on the server**, not from a client; it is a good check for noisy VMs. Compare the two: if intrinsic latency is a few microseconds, but `--latency` from the application host shows 2 ms, the network is the cost.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Measure from where the problem is seen. Run `redis-cli --latency` from the application host, check `SLOWLOG` and `LATENCY LATEST` on the server, and compare. If the server side is quiet but the application sees slow calls, look at the client: its connection pool, its timeouts, garbage-collection pauses in the JVM, thread starvation, or the number of calls per request.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Redis is single-threaded and fast, so why do some of my Redis calls take 50 ms? Common causes: network round trips and many small calls (fix with pipelining and multi-key commands); a slow O(N) command or big key blocking the single command thread so everyone queues behind it (find with `SLOWLOG`, fix the data model); a fork for persistence; swap or Transparent Huge Pages on the host; a client-side pool or GC pause. `SLOWLOG` only measures server execution, so you also compare it with client-side timings.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- One round trip per command caps a single connection at 1 / RTT operations per second; pipelining and multi-key commands remove most of that cost.
- Pipelines save time but are not atomic; keep batches to a few hundred or thousand commands.
- Blocking commands block only the caller, but the connection is occupied: use a dedicated connection and a finite timeout.
- Output buffers are unlimited for normal clients by default; avoid giant replies and watch `omem`.
- Diagnose with `SLOWLOG`, the latency monitor, `INFO latencystats` and `redis-cli --latency`; remember that slow commands delay everyone.

The fastest Redis call is the one you never make. Client-side caching lets an application keep a copy of hot values in its own memory and still be told by Redis when a value changes. The reads then cost nanoseconds instead of a network round trip, and Redis load drops. The feature is built on **RESP3**, the newer version of the Redis wire protocol, so we start there.

### RESP2 and RESP3

Clients and servers talk in **RESP** (REdis Serialization Protocol). RESP2 is the classic protocol that everything speaks by default. RESP3, available since Redis 6.0, adds richer reply types and, importantly, **push messages**: data that the server sends to a client without the client having asked for it, on the same connection.

A connection starts in RESP2. To switch, send `HELLO` with the protocol version; the server answers with information about itself:

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli -3
127.0.0.1:6379> HELLO 3
1# "server" => "redis"
2# "version" => "8.6.6"
3# "proto" => (integer) 3
4# "id" => (integer) 12
5# "mode" => "standalone"
6# "role" => "master"
7# "modules" => (empty array)
blocks.title: Switching a connection to RESP3

blocks.text:
What RESP3 changes for applications:

- **Typed replies.** Maps, sets, doubles, booleans and nulls get their own types, so `HGETALL` returns a real map instead of a flat array that the client must pair up, and `ZSCORE` returns a double. Client libraries do this decoding for you.
- **Push messages.** Pub/Sub messages and client-side caching invalidations arrive as pushes. In RESP3 one connection can run normal commands while also receiving pushes, which makes the single-connection design of client-side caching possible.
- `HELLO` **also authenticates and names the connection**: `HELLO 3 AUTH username password SETNAME` `catalog-service`.

Lettuce uses RESP3 by default when the server supports it and falls back to RESP2 otherwise; Spring Data Redis and Boot inherit that with Lettuce. For Jedis, check the default protocol of your version and set it explicitly if you need RESP3. Check your client's documentation before depending on RESP3 behaviour.

### The idea of client-side caching

Without it, every read of `product:77` goes to Redis. With it:

1. The application asks Redis for `product:77` and stores the value in a local map (for example Caffeine) inside the JVM.
2. Later reads are served from that map. No network.
3. When any client modifies `product:77`, Redis sends an **invalidation** to every connection that may have the key cached. Each of them deletes its local copy.
4. The next read misses locally, fetches the new value from Redis, and caches it again.

blocks.text:
The caching of values is the application's job. Redis only provides the invalidation signal, through the `CLIENT TRACKING` command.

### CLIENT TRACKING modes

#### Default mode

The connection turns tracking on, then reads keys normally. The server remembers, in a global **invalidation table**, which connections have read which keys. When a key is modified, deleted, expires or is evicted, the server pushes an invalidation message to the clients that read it, then forgets that key for those clients (they have to read it again to be tracked again). This mode costs server memory proportional to the number of tracked key and client pairs, and sends messages only to clients that actually may hold the key.

blocks.code:
# Connection A
127.0.0.1:6379> HELLO 3
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT TRACKING ON
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET product:77:name
"Wireless Mouse"
# Connection B
127.0.0.1:6379> SET product:77:name "Wireless Mouse v2"
OK
# Connection A receives a push message (shown here in simplified form)
1) "invalidate"
2) 1) "product:77:name"
blocks.title: Default tracking with two connections (RESP3)

blocks.text:
The push message is of type `invalidate`, carrying an array of key names; a null instead of an array means "everything": the server sends it after `FLUSHALL` and `FLUSHDB`, and the client should clear its whole local cache.

#### Broadcast mode

`CLIENT TRACKING ON BCAST PREFIX product: PREFIX category:` takes the opposite approach. The server remembers nothing per key. It simply notifies the connection whenever **any** key starting with a subscribed prefix is touched, whether or not the client ever read it. Server memory cost is almost nothing, but the client receives many more messages. It fits when the cached keys fall under a few clear prefixes and writes are not too frequent.

#### Opt-in and opt-out

By default, default mode tracks every key the connection reads, which can waste table space on values you do not cache. `OPTIN` flips this: only keys read by the command that immediately follows `CLIENT CACHING YES` are tracked. `OPTOUT` tracks everything except what follows `CLIENT CACHING NO`. Opt-in is the usual choice for applications that cache selectively. `OPTIN` and `OPTOUT` do not work with `BCAST`.

#### NOLOOP and REDIRECT

By default a client that modifies a key also receives the invalidation for it, which is wasteful if it just wrote the value into its cache. `NOLOOP` suppresses messages caused by the client's own writes. `REDIRECT client-id` sends invalidations to a different connection, which is how RESP2 clients can emulate tracking over Pub/Sub on the channel `__redis__:invalidate`. Modern code on RESP3 does not need it.
